creation.title: The Creation
creation.about: The Book of Genesis opens with God making the world in six days: light first, then the sky and the waters, the land and its plants, the sun, moon and stars, the creatures of sea and air and land, and last of all man and woman. On the seventh day He rested. Michelangelo painted the story along the spine of the Sistine Chapel ceiling between 1508 and 1512, beginning at the altar end with God dividing light from darkness.

adam-and-eve.title: Adam and Eve
adam-and-eve.about: God shaped Adam from the dust and breathed life into him, then made Eve from his rib while he slept, and set them in the Garden of Eden. They could eat of every tree but one, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Tempted by the serpent, Eve ate its fruit and gave it to Adam; their eyes were opened, they knew they were naked, and God drove them out of the garden to work the ground.

noah.title: Noah and the Flood
noah.about: Seeing the wickedness of the world, God resolved to destroy it by water, but told Noah, the one righteous man, to build an ark and take his family and a pair of every living creature into it. It rained forty days and nights and the waters covered the mountains. When they went down Noah sent out a raven and then a dove; when the dove came back with an olive leaf he knew the earth was dry. Noah gave thanks with a sacrifice, planted a vineyard, and once lay drunk and uncovered in his tent, where his sons found him.

abraham.title: Abraham
abraham.about: Abraham, the father of the people of Israel, left his homeland at God's call and was promised descendants as many as the stars. After he rescued his nephew Lot from four kings, Melchizedek, king of Salem and priest of God, came out to meet him with bread and wine and blessed him. Years later God tested Abraham by asking him to sacrifice Isaac, the son of his old age; an angel stopped his hand and a ram caught in a thicket was offered instead.

joseph.title: Joseph and his Brothers
joseph.about: Jacob loved his son Joseph more than his other sons and gave him a coat of many colours, and the brothers hated him for it and for his dreams of ruling over them. They sold him to traders bound for Egypt, dipped the coat in a goat's blood and brought it to their father, who believed a wild beast had killed him. Joseph rose to govern Egypt and in time forgave them.

moses.title: Moses
moses.about: Moses, born a Hebrew in Egypt and raised in Pharaoh's household, killed an Egyptian he saw beating a Hebrew slave and fled to Midian, where he defended the daughters of Jethro at a well and married one of them. God spoke to him from a bush that burned without being consumed and sent him back to lead his people out of Egypt. In the wilderness Korah and his followers rose against Moses and Aaron, and the earth opened and swallowed them.

scapegoat.title: The Scapegoat
scapegoat.about: On the Day of Atonement, the law of Leviticus told the high priest to lay his hands on the head of a goat, confess over it the sins of the people, and send it away into the wilderness to carry them off. Christians read it as a figure of Christ, who bore the sins of others.

david.title: David
david.about: David, the youngest son of Jesse, was a shepherd boy from Bethlehem who became Israel's greatest king. He killed the Philistine giant Goliath with a stone from his sling and cut off his head with the giant's own sword. King Saul's son Jonathan loved him as his own soul, and warned him of his father's jealousy with a sign of arrows shot in a field. As an outlaw David was turned from vengeance against the churl Nabal by Nabal's wise wife Abigail, whom he later married. He is also the traditional author of the Psalms.

elijah.title: Elijah
elijah.about: Elijah was a prophet of Israel in the reign of King Ahab. During a famine a widow of Zarephath shared her last meal with him, and when her son fell sick and died Elijah carried him to an upper room, stretched himself on the child three times and prayed, and the boy lived. Later, fleeing Queen Jezebel, he lay down under a juniper tree in the wilderness and asked to die, and an angel woke him and gave him bread and water.

esther.title: Esther
esther.about: Esther, a Jewish orphan raised by her cousin Mordecai, became queen to the Persian king Ahasuerus without revealing her people. When the minister Haman won a decree to destroy the Jews, Esther went before the king unbidden, though anyone who did so could be put to death unless he held out his golden sceptre. The Greek additions to the book, in the Apocrypha, tell how she fainted at his fierce look and how he leapt from his throne to hold her.

daniel.title: Daniel in the Lions' Den
daniel.about: Daniel, a young Jewish exile at the Persian court, kept praying to God after King Darius had forbidden prayer to anyone but himself. He was thrown into a den of lions and the mouth of the den sealed with a stone. In the morning the king found him unhurt: God had sent an angel to shut the lions' mouths.

prophets.title: The Prophets
prophets.about: The prophets of the Old Testament spoke for God to Israel, warning, consoling and foretelling. Christians read many of their words as pointing to Christ, which is why seven of them sit around the Sistine Chapel ceiling, alternating with five sibyls, the prophetesses of the pagan world.

sibyls.title: The Sibyls
sibyls.about: The sibyls were the prophetesses of the ancient Greek and Roman world, each tied to a shrine: Delphi, Erythrae, Cumae, Libya, Persia. Medieval Christians believed they too had foretold the coming of Christ, and so Michelangelo set five of them on the Sistine Chapel ceiling beside seven Hebrew prophets, each with a book or scroll of her oracles.

tree-of-jesse.title: The Tree of Jesse
tree-of-jesse.about: Isaiah foretold that a shoot would spring from the stem of Jesse, father of King David. Medieval artists drew it as a tree growing from the sleeping Jesse, with the kings of Israel in its branches and the Virgin and Christ at its top, to show Christ's descent from David.

judith.title: Judith and Holofernes
judith.about: The Book of Judith, in the Apocrypha, tells of a widow of the besieged town of Bethulia. When the Assyrian general Holofernes had cut off its water, Judith dressed in her finest clothes, went with her maid to his camp and won his trust. On the fourth night, when he lay drunk in his tent, she took down his sword, cut off his head, and carried it home in a bag of food. The Assyrians found his headless body in the morning and fled.

susanna.title: Susanna and the Elders
susanna.about: The History of Susanna, in the Apocrypha, tells of a virtuous wife in Babylon. Two elders who lusted after her hid in her garden while she bathed and threatened to swear she had lain with a young man unless she gave in to them. She refused, was condemned to death on their word, and was saved when the young Daniel questioned the two apart and caught them in their lie.

annunciation.title: The Annunciation
annunciation.about: In the Gospel of Luke the angel Gabriel is sent to Nazareth, to a young woman named Mary who was promised in marriage to Joseph, and tells her that she will bear a son and call him Jesus. Mary is troubled, asks how this can be, and accepts: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord." Painters show the angel kneeling with a lily, the flower of purity, and Mary often at her reading.

madonna.title: The Virgin and Child
madonna.about: The Virgin Mary holding the infant Jesus was the most painted subject of the Renaissance, made for altars, chapels and the private prayer of a household. The Gospels say little of the Child's infancy, so painters filled their pictures with signs: a pomegranate for the Resurrection, a goldfinch or a carnation for the Passion to come, a book for the prophecies, and the young John the Baptist, Christ's cousin, as the herald who would point him out.

magnificat.title: The Magnificat
magnificat.about: When Mary visited her cousin Elizabeth after the Annunciation, she answered Elizabeth's greeting with a song of praise that begins, in Latin, "Magnificat anima mea Dominum": "My soul doth magnify the Lord." It has been sung at evening prayer ever since.

nativity.title: The Nativity
nativity.about: Luke tells how Joseph and Mary travelled to Bethlehem for a census, found no room at the inn, and laid the newborn Jesus in a manger. An angel announced the birth to shepherds keeping watch over their flocks, a host of angels sang "Glory to God in the highest", and the shepherds went to Bethlehem to see the child.

magi.title: The Adoration of the Magi
magi.about: Matthew tells of wise men from the east who followed a star to Bethlehem, asking where the King of the Jews was born. They found the child with Mary his mother, worshipped him, and gave him gold, frankincense and myrrh. Later tradition made them three kings, named them Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar, and gave them the three ages of man and, in time, the three known continents. Florentine painters liked to put the Medici and their friends in the crowd.

circumcision.title: The Circumcision of Christ
circumcision.about: Following Jewish law, Jesus was circumcised on the eighth day after his birth and given the name the angel had told Mary. The church kept the feast on the first of January, and painters showed it as a ceremony in the Temple.

flight-into-egypt.title: The Flight into Egypt
flight-into-egypt.about: After the wise men left, an angel warned Joseph in a dream that King Herod meant to kill the child, and the Holy Family fled by night into Egypt. Herod, finding himself deceived, ordered every boy of two years and under in Bethlehem to be killed, the Massacre of the Innocents. Legends of the journey told of palm trees bending to give the family dates and of rests along the road.

finding-in-temple.title: The Finding of Christ in the Temple
finding-in-temple.about: When Jesus was twelve his parents took him to Jerusalem for Passover and started home without him. After three days of searching they found him in the Temple, sitting among the teachers, listening and asking questions, and all who heard him were astonished. To his mother's reproach he answered: "Wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?"

holy-family.title: The Holy Family
holy-family.about: The Holy Family is the Child with Mary and Joseph, often joined by Mary's mother, Saint Anne, and the infant John the Baptist with his mother Elizabeth. The Gospels give almost nothing of the years between the infancy and the ministry, so painters imagined quiet family scenes, often with signs of the Passion to come.

saint-anne.title: Saint Anne
saint-anne.about: Saint Anne, the mother of the Virgin Mary, is not named in the Bible; her story comes from the second-century Protevangelium of James, which tells how she and Joachim were childless until an angel promised them a daughter. She was much venerated in the late Middle Ages, and painters showed her with Mary and the Child as three generations together.

john-the-baptist.title: John the Baptist
john-the-baptist.about: John, the cousin of Jesus, was the last of the prophets. He lived in the wilderness of Judaea, dressed in camel's hair with a leather girdle and eating locusts and wild honey, and preached repentance, baptizing in the river Jordan. When he saw Jesus coming he said, "Behold the Lamb of God." Painters show him with a reed cross and a lamb or ram. He was imprisoned by Herod Antipas for condemning his marriage to Herodias, and beheaded at the request of her daughter Salome.

baptism.title: The Baptism of Christ
baptism.about: Jesus came from Galilee to the Jordan to be baptized by John. As he came up out of the water, the heavens opened, the Spirit of God came down like a dove, and a voice from heaven said, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

temptation.title: The Temptations of Christ
temptation.about: After his baptism Jesus fasted forty days in the wilderness, and the devil came to tempt him three times: to turn stones into bread, to throw himself from the pinnacle of the Temple, and to take all the kingdoms of the world in return for worshipping him. Each time Jesus answered with scripture, and the devil left him.

calling-of-apostles.title: The Calling of the Apostles
calling-of-apostles.about: Jesus chose his first followers from ordinary working men. Walking by the Sea of Galilee he saw the fishermen Simon Peter and his brother Andrew casting a net and said, "Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men." Later he saw Matthew, a tax collector, sitting at the receipt of custom, and called him too.

cleansing-temple.title: Christ Cleansing the Temple
cleansing-temple.about: Coming to Jerusalem for Passover, Jesus found the Temple courts full of men selling cattle, sheep and doves and changing money. He made a whip of cords, drove them all out and overturned the tables, saying they had made his Father's house a house of merchandise.

martha-and-mary.title: Martha and Mary
martha-and-mary.about: Luke tells how Jesus visited the house of two sisters: Martha busied herself serving, while Mary sat at his feet and listened. Martha complained, and Jesus answered that Mary had chosen the better part. Tradition made this Mary one with Mary Magdalene, and painters showed Martha persuading her worldly sister to turn from vanity.

mary-magdalene.title: Mary Magdalene
mary-magdalene.about: Mary Magdalene followed Jesus, stood at the foot of the cross, and was the first to see him risen. Western tradition merged her with the sinful woman who washed Jesus's feet with her tears and dried them with her hair, and with Mary of Bethany, making her the great example of the repentant sinner. The Golden Legend tells that she ended her life as a hermit in Provence, lifted up each day by angels.

lazarus.title: The Raising of Lazarus
lazarus.about: Lazarus of Bethany, the brother of Martha and Mary, fell sick and died, and had lain in the tomb four days when Jesus came. Jesus wept, had the stone taken away, and cried with a loud voice, "Lazarus, come forth," and the dead man came out, bound hand and foot in grave clothes.

salome.title: The Beheading of John the Baptist
salome.about: Herod Antipas had imprisoned John for condemning his marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife. At Herod's birthday feast Herodias's daughter, whom tradition names Salome, danced and pleased him so much that he swore to give her whatever she asked. Prompted by her mother, she asked for John's head on a charger, and Herod, unwilling to break his oath before his guests, sent an executioner to the prison.

last-supper.title: The Last Supper
last-supper.about: On the night before he died, Jesus ate the Passover meal with his twelve apostles. During supper he said, "One of you shall betray me," and each of them asked in turn, "Lord, is it I?" He then blessed and broke bread and gave them wine, saying "This is my body" and "This is my blood". Judas had already agreed to hand him over for thirty pieces of silver.

passion.title: The Passion of Christ
passion.about: The Passion is the suffering of Jesus from his arrest to his death. Judas led armed men to the garden of Gethsemane and singled him out with a kiss. That night Peter, warned he would deny his master three times before the cock crowed, did so. Pontius Pilate had Jesus scourged; the soldiers crowned him with thorns and mocked him; Pilate showed him to the crowd saying "Behold the man!" and gave him up to be crucified.

crucifixion.title: The Crucifixion
crucifixion.about: Jesus was crucified outside Jerusalem between two thieves. From the sixth hour to the ninth there was darkness over the land; then he cried with a loud voice, commended his spirit to his Father, and died. His mother, Mary Magdalene and the apostle John stood by the cross.

entombment.title: The Lamentation and Entombment
entombment.about: After the Crucifixion, Joseph of Arimathea, a secret follower, asked Pilate for the body, and with Nicodemus took it down from the cross, wound it in linen with myrrh and aloes, and laid it in a new tomb cut in the rock. Painters showed the mourning over the body, the Lamentation, and its carrying to the tomb, the Entombment.

emmaus.title: The Supper at Emmaus
emmaus.about: On the day of the Resurrection two disciples walking to the village of Emmaus were joined by a stranger who explained the scriptures to them. They asked him to stay and eat, and when he blessed and broke the bread their eyes were opened and they knew him as the risen Jesus, and he vanished from their sight.

doubting-thomas.title: The Incredulity of Saint Thomas
doubting-thomas.about: The apostle Thomas was not with the others when the risen Jesus first appeared to them, and said he would not believe unless he put his finger into the print of the nails and his hand into the wound in his side. Eight days later Jesus appeared again and told him to do so, and Thomas answered, "My Lord and my God."

conversion-of-paul.title: The Conversion of Saint Paul
conversion-of-paul.about: Saul of Tarsus was a zealous persecutor of the first Christians. On the road to Damascus a light from heaven struck him to the ground and a voice said, "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" Blinded, he was led into the city, where after three days a disciple restored his sight and baptized him. As Paul he became the great apostle to the Gentiles.

apostle-paul.title: Saint Paul the Apostle
apostle-paul.about: Paul carried the Christian faith across the Roman world and wrote the letters that make up much of the New Testament. Tradition says he was beheaded in Rome under Nero, and he is shown with the sword of his martyrdom and the book or letters of his teaching.

john-evangelist.title: Saint John the Evangelist
john-evangelist.about: John, the youngest of the apostles and "the disciple whom Jesus loved", was by tradition the author of the fourth Gospel and of the Book of Revelation, which he wrote in exile on the island of Patmos after visions of the end of the world. His sign is the eagle, the creature of the highest vision.

revelation.title: The Book of Revelation
revelation.about: The last book of the Bible records the visions of John on Patmos: letters to seven churches, the throne of God, the seven seals, the woman clothed with the sun, the last judgement when the sea gives up its dead, and the new Jerusalem. Its images have fed painters for centuries.

works-of-mercy.title: The Seven Works of Mercy
works-of-mercy.about: In the Gospel of Matthew, Jesus describes the last judgement: the blessed are those who fed the hungry, gave drink to the thirsty, welcomed the stranger, clothed the naked, visited the sick and those in prison, for "inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." The church added burying the dead to make seven.

death-of-the-virgin.title: The Death of the Virgin
death-of-the-virgin.about: The Bible says nothing of Mary's death. Legends gathered in the Golden Legend tell that an angel warned her three days before, that the apostles were carried miraculously from wherever they were preaching to be at her bedside, and that Christ came to receive her soul. The Catholic Church holds that she was then taken up body and soul into heaven, the Assumption.

awakening-conscience.title: The Awakening Conscience
awakening-conscience.about: Holman Hunt's picture is not from the Bible, but he framed it in scripture. A kept woman, sitting at the piano in the room her lover has taken for her, rises from his lap as the song they are singing, Thomas Moore's "Oft in the Stilly Night", recalls her childhood, and she sees through the window the garden and the light outside. On the frame Hunt carved a verse from Proverbs.

hope.title: Hope
hope.about: Hope is one of the three theological virtues with Faith and Charity, the "faith, hope, charity" of Saint Paul. Renaissance painters showed her as a woman reaching upward, and Burne-Jones, painting her in 1896 after the death of his friend William Morris, showed her chained and still reaching.

wings-of-the-morning.title: Wings of the Morning
wings-of-the-morning.about: The title comes from Psalm 139, in which the psalmist says there is nowhere he can go from God's presence: not to heaven, not to the grave, not even if he takes "the wings of the morning" to the far side of the sea. Hughes painted a winged figure of the dawn flying over the sea at first light.

work.title: Work
work.about: Ford Madox Brown spent thirteen years on this picture of navvies digging a drain in Hampstead, ringed by every class of Victorian society, from the idle rich on horseback to the ragged flower-seller. The two men standing on the right are the writers Thomas Carlyle and F. D. Maurice, the "brain-workers" who preached the dignity of labour. Brown carved four verses of scripture about work on the frame.

saint-george.title: Saint George and the Dragon
saint-george.about: George was a Christian soldier, probably martyred in Palestine around 303. The dragon story was added in the Middle Ages and made famous by the Golden Legend: at Silene in Libya a dragon was fed with the townspeople chosen by lot until the lot fell on the king's daughter, and George, riding by, wounded the beast, had the princess lead it into the town on her girdle, and slew it when the people agreed to be baptized. He became the patron saint of England, of soldiers and of chivalry.

saint-sebastian.title: Saint Sebastian
saint-sebastian.about: Sebastian was a Roman officer of the emperor Diocletian's guard who secretly helped Christians. When he was found out he was tied to a stake and shot with arrows and left for dead, but a Christian widow, named Irene in later tellings, came to bury him, found him alive and nursed him back to health. He confronted the emperor again and was beaten to death. Because arrows stood for the plague, he was prayed to against it.

saint-jerome.title: Saint Jerome
saint-jerome.about: Jerome (about 347–420) was the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin, the Vulgate used by the Western church for a thousand years. He spent years as a hermit in the Syrian desert, beating his breast with a stone in penance, and later ran a monastery in Bethlehem. The Golden Legend tells how a lame lion walked into the monastery and Jerome drew a thorn from its paw, after which it stayed with him. Painters show him as a hermit with his stone, as a scholar at his desk with a skull, and with his lion, often in the red hat of a cardinal, which he never was.

saint-augustine.title: Saint Augustine
saint-augustine.about: Augustine of Hippo (354–430), the greatest of the Latin church fathers, wrote the Confessions and The City of God. A late medieval letter, falsely said to be his, told how he was writing to Saint Jerome when his cell filled with light and a sweet smell, and he heard Jerome's voice and knew that Jerome had at that moment died.

saint-martin.title: Saint Martin and the Beggar
saint-martin.about: Martin was a young Roman cavalry officer, not yet baptized, when on a winter day at the gate of Amiens he met a beggar almost naked with cold. Having nothing else to give, he cut his military cloak in two with his sword and gave the man half. That night Christ appeared to him in a dream wearing the half cloak. Martin left the army and became bishop of Tours, one of the most loved saints of France.

saint-agnes.title: Saint Agnes
saint-agnes.about: Agnes was a Roman girl of about thirteen, martyred around 304 for refusing to marry and to sacrifice to the gods. Her name is close to agnus, the Latin for lamb, and she is always shown with a lamb, which, the Golden Legend says, appeared with her to her parents after her death.

saint-martina.title: Saint Martina
saint-martina.about: Martina was a Roman virgin martyr of the third century, little known before her relics were found in Rome in 1634. In El Greco's picture she appears with a lion, one of the beasts that, her legend says, refused to harm her.

saint-ildefonso.title: Saint Ildefonso
saint-ildefonso.about: Ildefonso was archbishop of Toledo in the seventh century and wrote a treatise defending the perpetual virginity of Mary. Legend says the Virgin appeared to him and gave him a chasuble from heaven. He was the patron of Toledo, El Greco's city.

saint-catherine.title: Saint Catherine of Alexandria
saint-catherine.about: Catherine was a learned princess of Alexandria who, by legend, outargued fifty philosophers sent by the emperor to shake her faith, and converted them. The emperor had her bound to a machine of spiked wheels, but an angel shattered it, and she was then beheaded. The "Catherine wheel" is named after her, and she is shown with the broken wheel, a sword and a crown.

saint-lucy.title: Saint Lucy
saint-lucy.about: Lucy was a young Christian of Syracuse in Sicily, martyred around 304. The Golden Legend says that when the governor Paschasius ordered her taken to a brothel, a thousand men and teams of oxen could not move her, fire would not burn her, and at last she was stabbed through the throat with a sword. Her name means light, and she is the patron of the blind.

saint-ursula.title: Saint Ursula
saint-ursula.about: Ursula was a British princess who, by legend, agreed to marry a pagan prince on condition that she first make a pilgrimage to Rome with eleven thousand virgin companions. On the way home they found Cologne besieged by the Huns, who killed them all. The Hun prince offered to marry Ursula, and when she refused he shot her with an arrow.

saint-barbara.title: Saint Barbara
saint-barbara.about: Barbara's pagan father shut her in a tower to keep her from suitors. While he was away she had the workmen make three windows in his bathhouse in place of two, in honour of the Trinity, and when he found she was a Christian he handed her over to be tortured and beheaded her himself, after which he was struck by lightning. She is shown with her tower and is the patron of artillerymen and miners.

mary-magdalene-legend.title: Mary Magdalene in the Wilderness
mary-magdalene-legend.about: The Golden Legend tells that after the Ascension Mary Magdalene was set adrift in a boat with other followers of Christ and came to Marseilles, where she converted Provence. She then withdrew to a desert cave for thirty years without food, and seven times a day angels lifted her into the air to hear the music of heaven, which was all the nourishment she needed.

saint-francis.title: Saint Francis of Assisi
saint-francis.about: Francis (1181/2–1226), son of a rich cloth merchant of Assisi, gave up everything to live in poverty and preach, and founded the Franciscan order. In 1224, praying on the mountain of La Verna, he saw a seraph with six wings in the form of a man crucified, and received in his own hands, feet and side the wounds of Christ, the stigmata. He is shown in a brown habit with a rope belt, often with a skull for meditation on death.

brother-conrad.title: Brother Conrad of Offida
brother-conrad.about: Conrad of Offida (died 1306) was a Franciscan friar of the Marches of Ancona. The Little Flowers of Saint Francis, a fourteenth-century book of tales of Francis and his followers, tells how Conrad prayed in the forest to feel something of the sweetness of Simeon holding the infant Christ, and the Virgin came and laid her son in his arms, while his friend Brother Peter watched from a distance.

saint-matthew.title: Saint Matthew
saint-matthew.about: Matthew the tax collector, called by Jesus from his counting table, became an apostle and, by tradition, the author of the first Gospel; his sign is an angel, or a winged man. The Golden Legend says he preached in Ethiopia and was killed at the altar after mass on the order of King Hirtacus, whose wish to marry the consecrated virgin Iphigenia he had opposed.

saint-peter.title: The Crucifixion of Saint Peter
saint-peter.about: Peter, the chief of the apostles, was martyred in Rome under Nero. Tradition, told in the Golden Legend, says he asked to be crucified head downward, not thinking himself worthy to die as his Lord had.

saint-andrew.title: The Crucifixion of Saint Andrew
saint-andrew.about: Andrew, Peter's brother, was crucified at Patras in Greece on the order of the proconsul Aegeas. The Golden Legend says he hung on the cross two days, preaching to the crowd, and when Aegeas, fearing the people, came to take him down, Andrew prayed to die there and the men who tried to untie him found their arms paralysed. The X-shaped "saltire" cross is a later tradition; Caravaggio painted an upright one.

saint-anthony.title: Saint Anthony Abbot
saint-anthony.about: Anthony of Egypt (about 251–356) is counted the father of monks. Living alone in the desert, he was assailed by demons who tempted him, beat him senseless and, in one famous story, lifted him into the air to torment him. Martin Schongauer's engraving of the scene, about 1470, was famous across Europe.

saint-zenobius.title: Saint Zenobius
saint-zenobius.about: Zenobius was an early bishop of Florence who died around 417. Born to a pagan family, he was converted and baptized as a young man, refused the bride his parents chose, and as bishop worked miracles, raising several dead children. When his body was carried to the cathedral it brushed against a dead elm tree, which burst into leaf in January. His feast was a great day in Florence.

saint-eulalia.title: Saint Eulalia
saint-eulalia.about: Eulalia of Mérida was a Spanish girl of about twelve martyred in 304 under Diocletian. The Roman poet Prudentius, writing about a century later, tells how a white dove flew from her mouth as she died and snow fell to cover her body in the forum.

merciful-knight.title: The Merciful Knight
merciful-knight.about: The legend of Saint John Gualbert, an eleventh-century Florentine knight, tells that on Good Friday he met the man who had killed his brother, alone in a narrow place. The murderer begged for mercy with his arms held out in the shape of a cross, and the knight spared him. Going on into a wayside chapel, he knelt before the crucifix, and the wooden Christ bent down from the cross and kissed him. John Gualbert later founded the Vallombrosan monks.

madonna-of-loreto.title: The Madonna of Loreto
madonna-of-loreto.about: Legend held that the house of the Virgin at Nazareth was carried by angels in 1294 to Loreto, on the Adriatic coast of Italy, which became one of the great pilgrim shrines of Europe.

madonna-of-the-rosary.title: The Madonna of the Rosary
madonna-of-the-rosary.about: Tradition says the Virgin gave the rosary, a chain of beads for counting prayers, to Saint Dominic, founder of the Dominican friars. Pictures of the Madonna of the Rosary show her with Dominic and other Dominican saints handing rosaries to the faithful.

saint-bartholomew.title: Saint Bartholomew
saint-bartholomew.about: Bartholomew was one of the twelve apostles. Tradition says he preached in India and Armenia and was flayed alive, so he is shown holding a knife or his own skin.

otto-magdeburg.title: Otto the Great and Magdeburg
otto-magdeburg.about: Otto I, duke of Saxony, king of Germany and from 962 emperor, founded the archbishopric of Magdeburg in 968 as the base for missions to the Slavs to the east. He was buried in its cathedral.

joan-of-arc.title: Joan of Arc
joan-of-arc.about: Joan (about 1412–1431), a peasant girl from Domrémy, heard the voices of saints telling her to save France from the English in the Hundred Years' War. She led the army that lifted the siege of Orléans in 1429 and saw Charles VII crowned at Reims, was captured, tried for heresy by a pro-English church court and burned at Rouen at nineteen. She was made a saint in 1920.

venus.title: Venus
venus.about: Venus, the Greek Aphrodite, goddess of love and beauty, was born, in one ancient telling, from the foam of the sea and carried ashore at Cyprus by the west wind, where the Hours, goddesses of the seasons, clothed her. She was the wife of the lame smith-god Vulcan and the lover of Mars, god of war, and the mother of Cupid. Renaissance thinkers made her a figure of divine as well as earthly love.

primavera.title: Primavera
primavera.about: Botticelli's great picture of spring has never been fully explained. In an orange grove, Venus stands at the centre with Cupid above; on the right Zephyr, the west wind, seizes the nymph Chloris, who turns into Flora, goddess of flowers, scattering roses; on the left the three Graces dance and Mercury lifts his staff to the clouds. The scene follows Ovid's calendar poem, the Fasti, in which Flora tells how Zephyr loved her, and the poetry of Poliziano, a friend of the Medici.

pallas-and-centaur.title: Pallas and the Centaur
pallas-and-centaur.about: Pallas Athena, the Roman Minerva, goddess of wisdom, grips by the hair a centaur, half man and half horse, the creature of unbridled passion. The picture is read as reason taming instinct. Her dress is patterned with the interlocking rings of the Medici.

calumny.title: The Calumny of Apelles
calumny.about: Apelles, the most famous painter of ancient Greece, was falsely accused of plotting against King Ptolemy and nearly put to death. In revenge he painted an allegory of Slander, which is lost. The Greek writer Lucian described it in detail, and Renaissance painters, urged on by the architect Alberti, tried to recreate it from his words.

virtues.title: The Virtues
virtues.about: The four cardinal virtues, Prudence, Justice, Fortitude and Temperance, and the three theological ones, Faith, Hope and Charity, were often painted as crowned women with their emblems. In 1470 the merchants' court of Florence ordered a set of seven for its hall; Piero del Pollaiuolo painted six, and the young Botticelli painted Fortitude, with her armour and mace.

liberal-arts.title: The Villa Lemmi Frescoes
liberal-arts.about: Two frescoes from a villa outside Florence, now in the Louvre, made for a wedding in the Tornabuoni family. In one, Venus and the three Graces bring gifts to a young woman; in the other, a young man is led before the Seven Liberal Arts, the subjects of a learned education: grammar, logic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and music. The young couple were long identified as Lorenzo Tornabuoni and Giovanna degli Albizzi, though this is not certain.

bacchus.title: Bacchus
bacchus.about: Bacchus, the Greek Dionysus, was the god of wine, revelry and release. Born from the thigh of his father Jupiter, he was raised by nymphs and travelled the world with his train of satyrs and maenads, teaching the growing of vines. His triumphal return from India, in a chariot drawn by panthers, was a favourite subject of Roman sarcophagi.

feast-of-the-gods.title: The Feast of the Gods
feast-of-the-gods.about: In Ovid's Fasti, the gods hold a rustic feast; the fertility god Priapus creeps up on the sleeping nymph Lotis, but the braying of Silenus's donkey wakes everyone and he is laughed away. Bellini painted the gods as country folk at a picnic, for the study of Alfonso d'Este, Duke of Ferrara.

laocoon.title: Laocoön
laocoon.about: Laocoön was the Trojan priest who warned his people not to trust the wooden horse the Greeks had left on the beach. As he sacrificed by the shore, two great serpents came out of the sea and crushed him and his two sons, and the Trojans, taking it as a sign of the gods' anger, dragged the horse into the city. Virgil tells the story in the second book of the Aeneid. An ancient marble group of the scene was dug up in Rome in 1506.

phaeton.title: Phaeton
phaeton.about: Phaeton, son of the sun god, begged his father to let him drive the chariot of the sun across the sky for one day. He could not hold the horses; they bolted, scorching the earth, and Jupiter struck him down with a thunderbolt to save the world. He fell blazing into the river Eridanus, and his sisters, mourning him, were turned into poplars.

venus-and-adonis.title: Venus and Adonis
venus-and-adonis.about: Venus fell in love with the beautiful young hunter Adonis and begged him to keep away from dangerous beasts. He would not listen, went out hunting, and was killed by a wild boar; from his blood Venus made the anemone grow. Titian's version, in which Adonis pulls away from her, was so popular that his studio made some thirty copies.

philemon-and-baucis.title: Philemon and Baucis
philemon-and-baucis.about: Jupiter and Mercury, disguised as travellers, went through Phrygia asking for shelter and were turned away from a thousand doors, until the poor old couple Philemon and Baucis took them in and shared what little they had. When the wine jug kept refilling itself the couple knew their guests were gods. The gods flooded the valley in punishment, turned the cottage into a temple, and granted the couple's wish to die together; they became an oak and a lime tree growing side by side.

proserpina.title: Proserpina
proserpina.about: Proserpina, the Greek Persephone, daughter of Ceres, goddess of the harvest, was gathering flowers in a meadow in Sicily when Pluto, god of the underworld, carried her off to be his queen. Ceres searched the world for her and in her grief let the crops fail, until Jupiter ordered her return. But Proserpina had eaten a few seeds of a pomegranate in the underworld, and so she must spend part of each year there: the winter, when nothing grows.

narcissus.title: Echo and Narcissus
narcissus.about: The nymph Echo, punished by Juno for her chatter, could only repeat the last words of others. She fell in love with the beautiful youth Narcissus, who scorned her, and she wasted away until only her voice was left. Narcissus in his turn, leaning over a clear pool to drink, fell in love with his own reflection, and pined beside it until he died and became the flower that bears his name.

medusa.title: Medusa
medusa.about: Medusa was one of the three Gorgons, with snakes for hair and a gaze that turned men to stone. The hero Perseus cut off her head while she slept, looking only at her reflection in his polished shield, and used it as a weapon; the goddess Minerva later set it on her shield. A painted Medusa's head on a shield was a fitting gift for a prince, a sign of victory over enemies.

perseus-and-andromeda.title: Perseus and Andromeda
perseus-and-andromeda.about: Queen Cassiopeia boasted that her daughter Andromeda was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, and to appease the sea god the princess was chained to a rock on the coast of Ethiopia as food for a sea monster. Perseus, flying home with the head of Medusa, saw her, fell in love, and killed the monster, and married her.

cadmus-and-harmonia.title: Cadmus and Harmonia
cadmus-and-harmonia.about: Cadmus, the founder of Thebes, killed a dragon sacred to Mars and sowed its teeth, from which armed men sprang up. Long afterwards, old and worn down by the misfortunes of their children, he and his wife Harmonia went into exile, and Cadmus prayed that if the dragon had been sacred he might become a serpent himself. He was changed as he spoke, and Harmonia, embracing him, asked to share his fate; both became gentle snakes.

orpheus-and-eurydice.title: Orpheus and Eurydice
orpheus-and-eurydice.about: Orpheus, the greatest of singers, lost his bride Eurydice to a snakebite on their wedding day. He went down into the underworld and sang so movingly that its rulers let her follow him back to life on one condition: that he not look back at her until they reached the upper air. Near the end he turned to see her, and she slipped back among the dead for ever.

circe.title: Circe
circe.about: Circe was an enchantress, daughter of the Sun, who lived on the island of Aeaea. In Homer's Odyssey she turned Ulysses's men into swine with a drugged drink; Ulysses, protected by a herb from Mercury, resisted her magic and made her restore them. In Ovid she loves the sea god Glaucus, who loves the nymph Scylla, and out of jealousy Circe poisons the pool where Scylla bathes, turning her into a monster girdled with dogs.

sirens.title: Ulysses and the Sirens
sirens.about: The Sirens sang so beautifully that sailors who heard them steered onto their rocks and died. Warned by Circe, Ulysses stopped his crew's ears with wax and had himself bound to the mast so that he could hear the song and live. Later writers made the Sirens beautiful women or mermaids, and the siren became a figure for any fatal enchantress.

hylas.title: Hylas and the Nymphs
hylas.about: Hylas was the young companion of Hercules on the voyage of the Argonauts. When the ship put in at the coast of Mysia he went to fetch water, and the nymphs of the spring, enchanted by his beauty, drew him down into the water. Hercules searched for him, calling his name, and was left behind by the Argo.

medea.title: Jason and Medea
medea.about: Jason sailed with the Argonauts to Colchis to win the Golden Fleece. King Aeetes set him impossible tasks, but the king's daughter Medea, a sorceress, fell in love with him and gave him a magic ointment that made him proof against fire and iron, and later helped him take the fleece. Their story ended in betrayal and murder, which Euripides made into his tragedy.

psyche.title: Cupid and Psyche
psyche.about: Psyche was a king's daughter so beautiful that Venus grew jealous and sent her son Cupid to make her love a monster; instead he fell in love with her himself, and visited her only in darkness. When she lit a lamp to see him, he fled, and she wandered the world seeking him, set impossible tasks by Venus. The last was to fetch a box of beauty from Proserpina in the underworld; curious, Psyche opened it and fell into a deathlike sleep, from which Cupid woke her. The tale is told in Apuleius's Golden Ass, of the second century.

helen.title: Helen of Troy
helen.about: Helen, the most beautiful woman in the world, was the wife of King Menelaus of Sparta. Her elopement with Paris, prince of Troy, brought the Greek kings to besiege Troy for ten years. In the Iliad the old men of the city, seeing her walk on the walls, say that no one could blame the Trojans and Greeks for suffering so long for such a woman.

cassandra.title: Cassandra
cassandra.about: Cassandra, daughter of King Priam of Troy, was given the gift of prophecy by Apollo, who loved her; when she refused him, he made it a curse: she would always foresee the truth and never be believed. She warned the Trojans against the wooden horse in vain and saw her city burn. Carried off as a captive by Agamemnon, she foretold his murder and her own at Mycenae.

andromache.title: Andromache
andromache.about: Andromache was the wife of Hector, the Trojan hero. In the Iliad, as Hector leaves for battle, she begs him to stay, and he answers that he knows Troy will fall and grieves most for her, whom some Greek will carry off to slavery to fetch water at a foreign spring. After the city's fall she was given as a captive to Achilles's son.

electra.title: Electra
electra.about: Electra was the daughter of Agamemnon, who was murdered on his return from Troy by his wife Clytemnestra and her lover Aegisthus. In Aeschylus's play The Libation Bearers she goes to her father's tomb with offerings and prays for vengeance, and there finds a lock of hair that tells her her exiled brother Orestes has come home.

night-and-sleep.title: Night and Sleep
night-and-sleep.about: In Hesiod's Theogony, the poem of the birth of the gods, Night is one of the first beings, born of Chaos. Among her children are the twin brothers Sleep and Death, who live in darkness at the edge of the world; Sleep wanders kindly over the earth, but Death has a heart of iron.

hesperides.title: The Garden of the Hesperides
hesperides.about: The Hesperides, "daughters of evening", were nymphs who tended a garden at the western edge of the world, where a tree of golden apples, the wedding gift of Earth to Juno, was guarded by a serpent, Ladon. Fetching the apples was one of the labours of Hercules.

graces.title: The Three Graces
graces.about: The three Graces, daughters of Jupiter, were goddesses of beauty, charm and joy: Aglaea, Euphrosyne and Thalia. Ancient artists showed them dancing or standing with their arms on each other's shoulders, the middle one seen from behind, a pose copied endlessly since.

aurora-and-tithonus.title: Aurora and Tithonus
aurora-and-tithonus.about: Aurora, the Greek Eos, goddess of the dawn, fell in love with the Trojan prince Tithonus and asked Jupiter to make him immortal, but forgot to ask that he stay young. He grew older and older, unable to die, until she shut him away in a room where he babbles on for ever.

diana.title: Diana
diana.about: Diana, the Greek Artemis, twin sister of Apollo, was the virgin goddess of the hunt, the moon and wild places, who roamed the woods with a band of nymphs sworn, like her, to chastity.

cupid.title: Cupid
cupid.about: Cupid, the Greek Eros, son of Venus, was the god of desire, shown as a winged boy with a bow whose arrows made gods and mortals fall in love. "Love conquers all," wrote Virgil, and painters made him triumphant over the arts and sciences, or asleep, or turning the wheel of time.

pan.title: Pan
pan.about: Pan, the goat-legged god of shepherds, flocks and wild country, played the reed pipes he made from the nymph Syrinx when she was turned into reeds to escape him. Burne-Jones painted him in a golden age, piping to a naked man and woman as if they were the first people in the world.

feast-of-peleus.title: The Feast of Peleus
feast-of-peleus.about: All the gods were invited to the wedding of the mortal Peleus and the sea nymph Thetis except Eris, goddess of strife, who threw among the guests a golden apple inscribed "for the fairest". Juno, Minerva and Venus each claimed it; Paris of Troy judged between them and gave it to Venus, who rewarded him with Helen, and so began the Trojan War.

phyllis-and-demophoon.title: Phyllis and Demophoön
phyllis-and-demophoon.about: Phyllis, a princess of Thrace, fell in love with Demophoön, son of Theseus, on his way home from Troy. He promised to return to her, but did not, and in despair she killed herself and was turned into an almond tree. When Demophoön came back at last and embraced the tree in grief, it burst into flower. The story is told in Ovid's Heroides and retold by Chaucer and Gower.

dryads.title: Nymphs and Dryads
dryads.about: In Greek belief every tree, spring, river and mountain had its nymph. Dryads and hamadryads were the nymphs of trees, a hamadryad living and dying with her own tree; naiads were nymphs of fresh water. Flora was the Roman goddess of flowers and the spring.

alexander.title: Alexander and Bucephalus
alexander.about: When Alexander the Great was a boy, a horse dealer brought his father, Philip of Macedon, a magnificent black horse that no one could ride. Alexander noticed that it shied at its own shadow, turned it toward the sun, calmed it and mounted it, and Philip wept with pride. Bucephalus carried Alexander through his conquests as far as India.

fortune.title: The Wheel of Fortune
fortune.about: Fortune, the goddess of chance, turns a great wheel on which men rise and fall, kings and slaves alike. The image comes chiefly from The Consolation of Philosophy, written by the Roman statesman Boethius in prison as he waited to be executed in 524, in which Philosophy reminds him that Fortune never stands still.

fisherman-and-syren.title: The Fisherman and the Syren
fisherman-and-syren.about: Goethe's ballad "Der Fischer" (1779) tells of a fisherman lured into the water by a mermaid who rises from the waves and sings to him of the peace of the deep: "half drew she him, half sank he in, and nevermore was seen." Leighton's painting of 1858 carries a line of it.

oracles.title: Priestesses and Oracles
oracles.about: The ancient world consulted oracles, priestesses or sacred voices that spoke for the gods, before any great undertaking. The most famous was the Pythia at Delphi; the Sibyls were their legendary sisters.

sorceresses.title: Enchantresses
sorceresses.about: The Victorians were fascinated by women of power in myth and legend: Circe, Medea, Morgan le Fay, Lilith, the Lady of the Lake. They painted them drawing magic circles, brewing potions and casting spells.

daphnephoria.title: The Daphnephoria
daphnephoria.about: The Daphnephoria, "laurel-bearing", was a festival held every ninth year at Thebes in honour of Apollo. A youth of good family led a procession carrying a pole of olive wood hung with laurel, flowers, and bronze balls standing for the sun, moon and stars, followed by a chorus of girls singing hymns. It is described by the late Greek writer Proclus.

amazons.title: The Amazons
amazons.about: The Amazons were a legendary nation of warrior women from the edges of the Greek world. Greek heroes, Hercules, Theseus and Achilles, each fought them, and the battle of Greeks and Amazons was a favourite subject of Athenian art in the fifth century BCE, after the Persian Wars: the civilised city against the wild outsiders.

egypt-afterlife.title: The Egyptian Afterlife
egypt-afterlife.about: Ancient Egyptians believed the dead must pass through the underworld to reach eternal life. The goddess Isis, wife of Osiris, lord of the dead, protected and guided them. The Book of the Dead, a collection of spells written on papyrus and buried with the mummy, helped the dead person through the dangers of the way and the weighing of the heart against the feather of truth.

bahram-gur.title: Bahram Gur and Azadeh
bahram-gur.about: Bahram Gur was a Sasanian king of Persia in the fifth century, famous as a hunter. A story told in Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, the Persian Book of Kings, says he went hunting with his harp-playing slave girl Azadeh riding behind him on his camel. She challenged him to shoot a gazelle so as to pin its hoof to its ear, and he did it with one arrow; but when she said it was the work of a devil, not a man, he threw her to the ground and rode her down under the camel.

ophelia.title: Ophelia
ophelia.about: Ophelia is the young noblewoman of Shakespeare's Hamlet (about 1600), daughter of the king's counsellor Polonius and sister of Laertes. Prince Hamlet courts her, then, feigning madness after his father's ghost reveals he was murdered, turns on her cruelly. When Hamlet kills her father by mistake she goes mad herself, wandering the court singing snatches of songs and giving out flowers, and soon after drowns in a brook while hanging garlands on a willow. Her death is not seen on stage: Queen Gertrude tells of it. Whether she fell or let herself drown is left open, and she is buried with doubtful rites.

hamlet.title: Hamlet
hamlet.about: Shakespeare's Hamlet, Prince of Denmark, learns from his father's ghost that his uncle Claudius murdered his father to take the throne and his mother. Torn between duty and doubt, he feigns madness and broods on life and death, most famously in the soliloquy "To be, or not to be". Hamlet was the great test of a tragic actor.

cordelia.title: Cordelia
cordelia.about: In Shakespeare's King Lear, the old king divides his kingdom among his three daughters according to how much each says she loves him. Goneril and Regan flatter him; the youngest, Cordelia, will say only that she loves him as a daughter should, and he disinherits her in a rage. The King of France marries her without a dowry, and as she leaves she bids her sisters, whom she sees through, to look after their father. When they turn him out into the storm she returns with an army to save him, too late.

measure-for-measure.title: Measure for Measure
measure-for-measure.about: In Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, the strict deputy Angelo, ruling Vienna in the Duke's absence, condemns young Claudio to death for getting his betrothed with child. Claudio's sister Isabella, about to become a nun, pleads for him, and Angelo offers to spare him if she will sleep with him. She refuses and goes to tell her brother, who first agrees she must refuse and then, terrified of death, begs her to save him. Meanwhile Mariana, whom Angelo jilted when her dowry was lost at sea, waits alone at a "moated grange"; the Duke uses her to trick Angelo.

juliet.title: Romeo and Juliet
juliet.about: In Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet, the daughter of the Capulets secretly marries Romeo of the rival house of Montague. When her parents insist she marry Count Paris, Friar Laurence gives her a potion that will make her seem dead for two days, so that she can be laid in the family tomb and escape with Romeo. On the morning of the wedding her family find her apparently dead. The message to Romeo goes astray, and both lovers die in the tomb.

orlando.title: Orlando and Rosalind
orlando.about: In Shakespeare's As You Like It, Orlando, wronged by his elder brother, flees to the Forest of Arden, where he hangs verses to Rosalind on the trees and carves her name in their bark. Rosalind, banished too and disguised as a youth called Ganymede, finds them, and teaches him how to woo her without revealing who she is.

mariana.title: Mariana
mariana.about: Mariana is the jilted woman of Shakespeare's Measure for Measure, left by Angelo when her dowry was lost at sea and living alone "at the moated grange". Tennyson made her the subject of a poem of 1830, a woman waiting endlessly for a lover who does not come, repeating "He cometh not". In "Mariana in the South" (1832) he moved her to a sun-baked house in Provence, where she prays to the Virgin.

lady-of-shalott.title: The Lady of Shalott
lady-of-shalott.about: Tennyson's poem (1832, revised 1842) tells of a lady under a curse who lives in a tower on an island in the river above Camelot. She may not look out of the window, and weaves into a tapestry the world she sees in a mirror. Seeing Sir Lancelot ride by in the mirror, she turns to look at him directly; the mirror cracks and the curse falls. She finds a boat, writes her name on it, lies down in it and floats down to Camelot, singing, and dies before she arrives. The poem drew on an Italian tale of the Lady of Escalot, who died for love of Lancelot.

cophetua.title: King Cophetua and the Beggar Maid
cophetua.about: An old ballad, printed in Percy's Reliques of 1765 and alluded to by Shakespeare, tells of an African king who cared nothing for women until he saw a beggar maid from his window, fell in love, and made her his queen. Tennyson retold it in a short poem, "The Beggar Maid".

millers-daughter.title: The Miller's Daughter
millers-daughter.about: Tennyson's poem (1832) is an old man's memory of courting and marrying a miller's daughter. Arthur Hughes exhibited April Love with lines from one of its songs about the small hurts of young love.

maud.title: Maud
maud.about: Tennyson's Maud (1855) is a long dramatic poem spoken by a brooding young man who falls in love with Maud, the daughter of the rich family he blames for his father's ruin. Its most famous section is the song "Come into the garden, Maud", sung as he waits for her at dawn after a ball: "And the soul of the rose went into my blood".

mermaid.title: The Mermaid
mermaid.about: In Tennyson's early poem "The Mermaid" (1830) a speaker imagines the life of a mermaid, singing alone and combing her hair under the sea. Waterhouse painted his mermaid as his diploma picture for the Royal Academy in 1900.

arthur.title: King Arthur
arthur.about: The legends of Arthur and his knights were gathered into English prose by Sir Thomas Malory in Le Morte d'Arthur (printed 1485) and retold for the Victorians by Tennyson in the Idylls of the King. They tell how the wizard Merlin served Arthur until the enchantress Nimue, or Vivien, learned his secrets and shut him in a rock; how Sir Tristram loved Isolde, the wife of King Mark of Cornwall, and was killed by Mark as he played the harp before her; and how Arthur, mortally wounded in his last battle, was carried away by three queens in a barge to the island valley of Avalon, to be healed and one day return.

belle-dame.title: La Belle Dame sans Merci
belle-dame.about: Keats's ballad (1819) begins with a question to a pale knight loitering by a lake in winter. He answers that he met a beautiful lady in the meadows, "a faery's child", set her on his horse, and was taken to her elfin grot and lulled asleep; there he dreamed of pale kings and warriors crying that the lovely lady without pity had him in thrall, and woke alone on the cold hillside. The title, "the beautiful lady without mercy", comes from a medieval French poem.

isabella.title: Isabella, or the Pot of Basil
isabella.about: Keats's poem (1820) retells a tale from Boccaccio's Decameron. Isabella, the sister of two rich merchants of Florence, loves their clerk Lorenzo. The brothers murder him and tell her he has gone abroad, but his ghost tells her where he lies. She digs up his head, hides it in a pot of basil, and waters the plant with her tears until her brothers steal it, and she dies of grief.

lamia.title: Lamia
lamia.about: Keats's Lamia (1820) is a serpent turned by Hermes into a beautiful woman. She enchants the young Corinthian Lycius, who meets her on the road and lives with her in a magic palace; at their wedding feast the philosopher Apollonius sees through her, and she vanishes, and Lycius dies.

manfred.title: Manfred
manfred.about: Byron's dramatic poem Manfred (1817) is about a nobleman tormented by guilt for some nameless sin connected with the woman he loved, Astarte. He summons spirits but cannot win forgetfulness from them, and on the cliffs of the Jungfrau tries to throw himself down, until a chamois hunter seizes him and leads him to safety.

don-juan.title: Don Juan and Haidée
don-juan.about: In the second canto of Byron's Don Juan (1819), the young Spaniard is shipwrecked and washed up half dead on a Greek island. He is found by Haidée, the daughter of a pirate, and her maid Zoe, who hide him in a cave and nurse him back to life. He and Haidée fall in love, until her father comes home.

black-brunswicker.title: The Black Brunswicker
black-brunswicker.about: The Black Brunswickers were a corps of German volunteers raised by Frederick William, Duke of Brunswick, against Napoleon, who wore black in mourning for their country and a silver death's head on their caps. On the eve of Waterloo, while their officers were at the Duchess of Richmond's ball in Brussels, news came that the French were advancing; the Duke was killed at Quatre Bras two days before the battle. Byron put the ball and the Duke into Childe Harold's Pilgrimage.

rossetti-poems.title: Rossetti's Picture Sonnets
rossetti-poems.about: Dante Gabriel Rossetti was a poet as well as a painter, and wrote sonnets for many of his pictures, sometimes on the frame itself, so that each explains the other. Several were gathered in his Poems (1870) and Ballads and Sonnets (1881).

lilith.title: Lilith
lilith.about: In Jewish legend Lilith was Adam's first wife, made from the earth as he was, who would not be subject to him and left Eden, becoming a demon who preys on men and children. Rossetti made her a figure of sensual beauty that ensnares, and wrote a sonnet, "Body's Beauty", for the painting. The frame also carried lines from Shelley's translation of Goethe's Faust warning against her hair.

beatrice.title: Dante and Beatrice
beatrice.about: Beatrice Portinari (1266–1290) was the Florentine woman Dante loved from childhood. In the Vita Nuova (about 1294), his book of poems with prose, he tells how he first saw her when they were both nine, how her greeting in the street filled him with bliss, and how she died at twenty-four. In the Divine Comedy she becomes his guide through Paradise. Rossetti, named after Dante, translated the Vita Nuova and painted its scenes again and again.

dante.title: Dante Alighieri
dante.about: Dante Alighieri (1265–1321), the greatest poet of Italy, was exiled from Florence for his politics in 1302 and wrote the Divine Comedy in exile: a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, guided first by the poet Virgil and then by Beatrice. He is usually shown in profile in a red hood and a laurel wreath.

francesca.title: Paolo and Francesca
francesca.about: In the fifth canto of Dante's Inferno, among the souls of the lustful whirled for ever on a dark wind, Dante meets Francesca da Rimini, who was married to the lame Gianciotto Malatesta and fell in love with his younger brother Paolo. She tells how they were reading together the romance of Lancelot and Guinevere, and at the moment of the lovers' kiss they kissed; her husband found them and killed them both.

gates-of-hell.title: The Gates of Hell
gates-of-hell.about: In 1880 Rodin was asked to make a bronze doorway for a planned museum of decorative arts in Paris. He took Dante's Inferno as his subject and worked on it for the rest of his life, filling the doors with nearly two hundred figures; many of his most famous sculptures began there. Above the doors sits The Thinker, first called The Poet, Dante brooding over his work, and over the gates of Dante's Hell are written the words that end "Abandon all hope, ye who enter here."

pia.title: La Pia de' Tolomei
pia.about: In the fifth canto of Dante's Purgatory, among those who died by violence, a woman speaks only a few lines: she is Pia of Siena, who died in the Maremma, the marshy coast, and the one who married her knows how. Commentators said that her husband Nello della Pietra shut her in his castle there and had her killed, or let the fever of the marshes kill her. Rossetti painted her gazing out from the battlements, fingering her wedding ring, with Jane Morris as the model.

leah-and-rachel.title: Leah and Rachel
leah-and-rachel.about: In Dante's Purgatory the poet dreams of Leah gathering flowers to make herself a garland, while her sister Rachel sits all day before her mirror. They stand for the active and the contemplative life. Leah's words "mia suora Rachel" mean "my sister Rachel".

fiammetta.title: Fiammetta
fiammetta.about: Fiammetta, "little flame", was the name Boccaccio gave to the woman he loved, traditionally said to be a lady of Naples, though no such person has been traced, and to one of the ten storytellers of his Decameron. Rossetti translated two of Boccaccio's sonnets about her, "Of Fiammetta Singing" and "Of his Last Sight of Fiammetta", and wrote a sonnet of his own for a vision of her among apple blossom.

petrarch-laura.title: Petrarch and Laura
petrarch-laura.about: The poet Francesco Petrarca first saw Laura in the church of Saint Clare at Avignon on Good Friday, 6 April 1327, and loved her for the rest of his life, though she was married to another. She died of the plague exactly twenty-one years later. His poems to her, the Canzoniere, set the pattern for the love sonnet across Europe.

decameron.title: The Decameron
decameron.about: In Boccaccio's Decameron (about 1353), seven young women and three young men escape the Black Death in Florence in 1348 to a villa in the hills, and to pass the time each tells a story every day for ten days: a hundred tales of love, wit and fortune. Each day has a king or queen who sets the theme.

nastagio.title: Nastagio degli Onesti
nastagio.about: The eighth story of the fifth day of the Decameron. Nastagio, a young man of Ravenna, is scorned by the lady he loves. Wandering in the pine forest of Classe, he sees a naked woman pursued by a knight with hounds, who kills her and feeds her heart to the dogs; the ghost knight explains that she scorned him in life, and that the hunt is repeated every Friday as their punishment. Nastagio holds a banquet on that spot the next Friday; his lady sees the vision, takes the lesson, and marries him.

cymon.title: Cymon and Iphigenia
cymon.about: The first story of the fifth day of the Decameron. Cimone, a rich young Cypriot so loutish he was called "the brute", comes upon the beautiful Efigenia asleep in a wood, and love for her makes him wise, courteous and learned. Dryden retold it in verse as Cymon and Iphigenia.

ansaldo.title: Messer Ansaldo's Garden
ansaldo.about: The fifth story of the tenth day of the Decameron. The lady Dianora, to be rid of Messer Ansaldo's courtship, promises herself to him if he can make her a garden in January as fair as in May. He hires a magician who does it. Her husband, hearing of her promise, tells her to keep it; Ansaldo, moved by the husband's generosity, releases her, and the magician releases Ansaldo from his fee.

bocca-baciata.title: Bocca Baciata
bocca-baciata.about: Rossetti took his title from an Italian proverb that ends one of the Decameron's bawdier tales, of a princess who passed through many men's hands and was still married as a maid: "Bocca baciata non perde ventura, anzi rinnova come fa la luna" — the mouth that has been kissed loses none of its fortune, but renews itself as the moon does. He wrote it on the back of the picture.

rosamund.title: Fair Rosamund
rosamund.about: Rosamund Clifford was the mistress of King Henry II of England in the 1170s. Legend said he hid her from his jealous queen, Eleanor of Aquitaine, in a bower at Woodstock reached through a maze, but the queen found the way in by following a silken thread and forced her to choose between a dagger and a cup of poison. The story was told in an old ballad by Thomas Deloney, printed in Percy's Reliques.

gather-rosebuds.title: Gather Ye Rosebuds
gather-rosebuds.about: Robert Herrick's poem "To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time" (1648) urges young women to enjoy their youth and marry while they can, for time flies and the rose that blooms today will be dying tomorrow.

love-among-ruins.title: Love Among the Ruins
love-among-ruins.about: Burne-Jones took the title from a poem by Robert Browning (1855), in which a lover crossing quiet pastures where a great city once stood, its glory and wars forgotten, thinks of the girl waiting for him in the one ruined tower that remains, and concludes "Love is best".

night-with-stars.title: Night with Her Train of Stars
night-with-stars.about: The title comes from W. E. Henley's poem "Margaritae Sorori" (1886), in which the poet watches evening fall over an old city and asks that his own death come as gently: "Night with her train of stars / And her great gift of sleep." The poem was often read at funerals. Hughes painted Night as a winged woman carrying sleeping children through the sky.

sidonia.title: Sidonia von Bork
sidonia.about: Sidonia von Bork (1548–1620) was a Pomeranian noblewoman executed as a witch. Wilhelm Meinhold made her the heroine of a lurid historical novel, Sidonia the Sorceress (1847), translated into English by Lady Wilde, Oscar Wilde's mother, which the Pre-Raphaelites loved. Meinhold described a portrait of her in her youthful beauty, a gold net over her hair, and Burne-Jones painted her from his words.

segur-blondine.title: Blondine, Bonne-Biche and Beau-Minon
segur-blondine.about: From the Comtesse de Ségur's New Fairy Tales (1857). Princess Blondine, neglected by her wicked stepmother, is lost in the enchanted Forest of Lilacs and raised for seven years by a white doe, Bonne-Biche, and a white cat, Beau-Minon, in their palace. Through her disobedience she loses them, and after long penance a tortoise carries her, for six months, to the fairy who can tell her their fate. In the end the doe and the cat are restored as the fairy Bienveillante and her son, Prince Parfait, whom Blondine marries.

segur-henry.title: Good Little Henry
segur-henry.about: From the Comtesse de Ségur's New Fairy Tales (1857). Henry, a poor boy whose mother is dying, is told by the fairy Bienfaisante that only the plant of life, which grows on top of a far mountain, can save her. On the way he helps everyone who asks him: he harvests the grapes of a giant who lets him through his wall, and at the summit the little Doctor of the fairies' garden gives him the plant. His mother is cured and Henry rewarded.

segur-rosette.title: Princess Rosette
segur-rosette.about: From the Comtesse de Ségur's New Fairy Tales (1857). Rosette, the youngest princess, is sent away by parents who do not love her and brought up in the country by her fairy godmother. Invited to a neighbouring king's court with her jealous sisters, she outshines them with the magic gowns and jewels her godmother gives her, and Prince Charmant falls in love with her.

segur-mouse.title: The Little Grey Mouse
segur-mouse.about: From the Comtesse de Ségur's New Fairy Tales (1857). Rosalie has been warned that her curiosity will put her in the power of a wicked fairy who appears as a little grey mouse. Again and again she gives way to it; at the palace of the prince who loves her she tears the cloth that hides a marvellous tree, and brings ruin on the palace.

segur-ourson.title: Ourson
segur-ourson.about: From the Comtesse de Ségur's New Fairy Tales (1857). Ourson, "little bear", is born covered with the fur of a bear through the spite of a wicked fairy, but is good and gentle. He grows up with Violette, a little girl found in the woods, who loves him; at last, to free him, she takes the bear's skin on herself, and the good fairy restores them both.

goody-two-shoes.title: Goody Two-Shoes
goody-two-shoes.about: The History of Little Goody Two-Shoes, published in London in 1765, possibly by Oliver Goldsmith, is the story of Margery Meanwell, a poor orphan so delighted when given a pair of shoes that she shows everyone her "two shoes". She teaches herself to read, becomes a teacher, and marries well. Walter Crane illustrated it as a picture book in the 1870s.

lucretia.title: Lucretia
lucretia.about: Livy tells that in 509 BCE Sextus Tarquinius, son of the last king of Rome, came by night to the house of Lucretia, the virtuous wife of his kinsman Collatinus, and violated her under threat of death and dishonour. She sent for her husband and father, told them what had happened, made them swear vengeance, and stabbed herself. Lucius Junius Brutus drew the knife from the wound and swore to drive out the kings; the revolt that followed founded the Roman Republic. For the Renaissance she was the model of the chaste wife and of the citizen's duty to resist tyranny.

virginia.title: Virginia
virginia.about: Livy tells that around 450 BCE Appius Claudius, one of the ten magistrates then ruling Rome, lusted after Virginia, the daughter of a plebeian centurion, and had a client of his claim her in court as his slave. When Appius ruled for the claim, her father Verginius, seeing no other way to save her from him, killed her with a knife snatched from a butcher's stall. The people rose, the ten were overthrown, and the Republic restored.

scipio.title: The Continence of Scipio
scipio.about: After the Roman general Publius Cornelius Scipio (later Africanus) took New Carthage in Spain in 209 BCE, his soldiers brought him a beautiful captive. Learning that she was betrothed to a young Celtiberian prince, Allucius, Scipio returned her untouched, and gave her parents' ransom gold to the couple as a wedding gift. The story, told by Livy, became a model of a ruler's self-restraint.

decius-mus.title: Decius Mus
decius-mus.about: In 340 BCE, before a battle with the Latins near Mount Vesuvius, both Roman consuls dreamed that the side whose general offered himself to the gods of the dead would win. Publius Decius Mus told his troops of the dream, and when his wing began to give way, devoted himself in a solemn rite and rode alone into the enemy ranks to his death; the Romans won. Rubens designed a series of tapestries on his life around 1616.

agrippina.title: Germanicus and Agrippina
agrippina.about: Germanicus (15 BCE–19 CE), adopted son of the emperor Tiberius, was a popular general whose sudden death in Syria was blamed on poison. His wife Agrippina the Elder, granddaughter of Augustus, carried his ashes back to Rome and became the emperor's enemy. Their son was the emperor Caligula. Rubens painted their heads in profile, overlapping, like a pair on an ancient cameo or coin.

honorius.title: The Emperor Honorius
honorius.about: Honorius was emperor of the Western Roman Empire from 395 to 423, a weak ruler who shut himself up in Ravenna while Alaric and the Goths sacked Rome in 410. The historian Procopius tells that when a servant told him Rome had perished, he cried out in distress, thinking it was his favourite chicken, which was called Roma.

burghers-of-calais.title: The Burghers of Calais
burghers-of-calais.about: In 1347, after a siege of eleven months in the Hundred Years' War, Edward III of England offered to spare the starving people of Calais if six of their leading citizens came out to him barefoot, with halters round their necks and the keys of the town, to be put to death. Eustache de Saint-Pierre volunteered first, and five more followed. The chronicler Froissart tells that the king was set on hanging them until his pregnant queen, Philippa of Hainault, knelt and begged for their lives. Calais asked Rodin for a monument in 1884; he made the six as individual men going to their deaths, not heroes.

princes-in-the-tower.title: The Princes in the Tower
princes-in-the-tower.about: Edward V, aged twelve, and his younger brother Richard, Duke of York, the sons of Edward IV, were lodged in the Tower of London in 1483 by their uncle, who then took the throne as Richard III. The boys were never seen again. Thomas More and Shakespeare told that Richard had them smothered by order of Sir James Tyrrell; what happened is still argued.

order-of-release.title: The Order of Release, 1746
order-of-release.about: After the defeat of the Jacobite rising of 1745 at Culloden in 1746, many Highlanders who had fought for Bonnie Prince Charlie were imprisoned. Millais imagined a wife who has won her husband's release, bringing the signed order to the jailer with their child in her arms and the family dog leaping up to greet him.

north-west-passage.title: The North-West Passage
north-west-passage.about: For three centuries British sailors sought a sea route round the north of America to the Pacific. In 1845 Sir John Franklin's expedition disappeared in the Arctic with all 129 men, and searches for it went on for decades. Millais's picture was painted in 1874 as a new Arctic expedition was being prepared, and an old sea captain declares that it might be done, and England ought to do it.

last-of-england.title: The Last of England
last-of-england.about: In the early 1850s hundreds of thousands of people a year left Britain for Australia and America. Ford Madox Brown, poor and thinking of emigrating himself, painted a young couple on the deck of a ship leaving the white cliffs of Dover, their faces set. He and his wife Emma were the models; their friend the sculptor Thomas Woolner had just sailed for the gold fields of Australia.

holy-fire.title: The Miracle of the Holy Fire
holy-fire.about: Every Easter Saturday in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, the Greek Orthodox patriarch goes alone into the tomb of Christ and comes out with candles lit, it is held, by fire from heaven, and the flame is passed through a dense, ecstatic crowd. Holman Hunt, a fervent Protestant, saw the ceremony in 1892 and thought it a fraud, and painted it as a satire.

royal-wedding-1863.title: The Royal Wedding of 1863
royal-wedding-1863.about: On 10 March 1863 Albert Edward, Prince of Wales, later Edward VII, married Princess Alexandra of Denmark. London was illuminated that night, and the crowd on London Bridge was so great that people were crushed.

may-morning.title: May Morning at Oxford
may-morning.about: At six on the morning of the first of May each year, the choir of Magdalen College, Oxford, sings a Latin hymn from the top of the college tower, a custom going back at least to the seventeenth century, while crowds listen below.

cimabue.title: Cimabue's Madonna
cimabue.about: Giorgio Vasari, in his Lives of the Artists (1550), tells that when the Florentine painter Cimabue finished a great Madonna for the church of Santa Maria Novella, the people thought it so marvellous that they carried it from his house to the church in procession with trumpets. The young Giotto, his pupil, was said to have walked beside him. Modern scholars give the Rucellai Madonna to Duccio, not Cimabue.

converted-family.title: A Converted British Family
converted-family.about: Holman Hunt imagined a family of ancient Britons, newly Christian, hiding a missionary from a mob of druids, the priests of the old religion. The subject was a Victorian invention, a compliment to Britain's early faith.

gen-light.text: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep. And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters. And God said, Let there be light: and there was light. And God saw the light, that it was good: and God divided the light from the darkness. And God called the light Day, and the darkness he called Night. And the evening and the morning were the first day.

gen-sun-moon.text: And God said, Let the earth bring forth grass, the herb yielding seed, and the fruit tree yielding fruit after his kind, whose seed is in itself, upon the earth: and it was so. And the earth brought forth grass, and herb yielding seed after his kind, and the tree yielding fruit, whose seed was in itself, after his kind: and God saw that it was good. … And God said, Let there be lights in the firmament of the heaven to divide the day from the night; and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days, and years: And let them be for lights in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth: and it was so. And God made two great lights; the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also. And God set them in the firmament of the heaven to give light upon the earth, And to rule over the day and over the night, and to divide the light from the darkness: and God saw that it was good.

gen-adam.text: So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them. … And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

gen-breath.text: And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.

gen-eve.text: And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man. And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.

gen-fall.text: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat. And the eyes of them both were opened, and they knew that they were naked; and they sewed fig leaves together, and made themselves aprons. … Therefore the LORD God sent him forth from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from whence he was taken. So he drove out the man; and he placed at the east of the garden of Eden Cherubims, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to keep the way of the tree of life.

gen-eve-shame.text: And when the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, she took of the fruit thereof, and did eat, and gave also unto her husband with her; and he did eat.
