Her hair was long, her foot was light,
And her eyes were wild.

I made a garland for her head,
And bracelets too, and fragrant zone;
She look'd at me as she did love,
And made sweet moan.

I set her on my pacing steed,
And nothing else saw all day long,
For sidelong would she bend, and sing
A faery's song.
belle-dame.cite: Keats, "La Belle Dame sans Merci", stanzas IV–VI

isabella-i.text:
Fair Isabel, poor simple Isabel!
Lorenzo, a young palmer in Love's eye!
They could not in the self-same mansion dwell
Without some stir of heart, some malady;
They could not sit at meals but feel how well
It soothed each to be the other by;
They could not, sure, beneath the same roof sleep
But to each other dream, and nightly weep.
isabella-i.cite: Keats, "Isabella; or, the Pot of Basil", stanza I

isabella-liii.text:
And she forgot the stars, the moon, and sun,
And she forgot the blue above the trees,
And she forgot the dells where waters run,
And she forgot the chilly autumn breeze;
She had no knowledge when the day was done,
And the new morn she saw not: but in peace
Hung over her sweet Basil evermore,
And moisten'd it with tears unto the core.
isabella-liii.cite: Keats, "Isabella; or, the Pot of Basil", stanza LIII

lamia.text:
Leave thee alone! Look back! Ah, Goddess, see
Whether my eyes can ever turn from thee!
For pity do not this sad heart belie—
Even as thou vanishest so I shall die. …

manfred.text:
Chamois Hunter. Friend! have a care,
Your next step may be fatal!—for the love
Of Him who made you, stand not on that brink!

Manfred. (not hearing him).
Such would have been for me a fitting tomb;
My bones had then been quiet in their depth;
They had not then been strewn upon the rocks
For the wind's pastime—as thus—thus they shall be—
In this one plunge.—Farewell, ye opening Heavens!
Look not upon me thus reproachfully—
You were not meant for me—Earth! take these atoms!

[As MANFRED is in act to spring from the cliff, the
CHAMOIS HUNTER seizes and retains him with a sudden grasp.

Chamois Hunter. Hold, madman!—though aweary of thy life,
Stain not our pure vales with thy guilty blood:
Away with me—I will not quit my hold.

don-juan.text:
His eyes he open’d, shut, again unclosed,
For all was doubt and dizziness; he thought
He still was in the boat and had but dozed,
And felt again with his despair o’erwrought,
And wish’d it death in which he had reposed;
And then once more his feelings back were brought,
And slowly by his swimming eyes was seen
A lovely female face of seventeen.

’Twas bending close o’er his, and the small mouth
Seem’d almost prying into his for breath;
And chafing him, the soft warm hand of youth
Recall’d his answering spirits back from death;
And, bathing his chill temples, tried to soothe
Each pulse to animation, till beneath
Its gentle touch and trembling care, a sigh
To these kind efforts made a low reply.

Then was the cordial pour’d, and mantle flung
Around his scarce-clad limbs; and the fair arm
Raised higher the faint head which o’er it hung;
And her transparent cheek, all pure and warm,
Pillow’d his death-like forehead; then she wrung
His dewy curls, long drench’d by every storm;
And watch’d with eagerness each throb that drew
A sigh from his heaved bosom—and hers, too.
don-juan.cite: Byron, Don Juan, Canto II, stanzas 111–113

harold-revelry.text:
There was a sound of revelry by night,
And Belgium's capital had gathered then
Her Beauty and her Chivalry, and bright
The lamps shone o'er fair women and brave men;
A thousand hearts beat happily; and when
Music arose with its voluptuous swell,
Soft eyes looked love to eyes which spake again,
And all went merry as a marriage bell;
But hush! hark! a deep sound strikes like a rising knell!

Did ye not hear it?—No; 'twas but the wind,
Or the car rattling o'er the stony street;
On with the dance! let joy be unconfined;
No sleep till morn, when Youth and Pleasure meet
To chase the glowing Hours with flying feet.
But hark!—that heavy sound breaks in once more,
As if the clouds its echo would repeat;
And nearer, clearer, deadlier than before!
Arm! arm! it is—it is—the cannon's opening roar!

Within a windowed niche of that high hall
Sate Brunswick's fated chieftain; he did hear
That sound, the first amidst the festival,
And caught its tone with Death's prophetic ear;
And when they smiled because he deemed it near,
His heart more truly knew that peal too well
Which stretched his father on a bloody bier,
And roused the vengeance blood alone could quell:
He rushed into the field, and, foremost fighting, fell.
harold-revelry.cite: Byron, Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto III, stanzas 21–23

rossetti-sea-spell.text:
Her lute hangs shadowed in the apple-tree,
While flashing fingers weave the sweet-strung spell
Between its chords; and as the wild notes swell,
The sea-bird for those branches leaves the sea.
But to what sound her listening ear stoops she?
What netherworld gulf-whispers doth she hear,
In answering echoes from what planisphere,
Along the wind, along the estuary?
She sinks into her spell: and when full soon
Her lips move and she soars into her song,
What creatures of the midmost main shall throng
In furrowed surf-clouds to the summoning rune:
Till he, the fated mariner, hears her cry,
And up her rock, bare-breasted, comes to die?

rossetti-fiammetta.text:
Behold Fiammetta, shown in Vision here.
Gloom-girt 'mid Spring-flushed apple-growth she stands;
And as she sways the branches with her hands,
Along her arm the sundered bloom falls sheer,
In separate petals shed, each like a tear;
While from the quivering bough the bird expands
His wings. And lo! thy spirit understands
Life shaken and shower'd and flown, and Death drawn near.
All stirs with change. Her garments beat the air:
The angel circling round her aureole
Shimmers in flight against the tree's grey bole:
While she, with reassuring eyes most fair,
A presage and a promise stands; as 'twere
On Death's dark storm the rainbow of the Soul.
rossetti-fiammetta.cite: Rossetti, "Fiammetta" (sonnet for A Vision of Fiammetta, 1878)

rossetti-found.text:
"There is a budding morrow in midnight:"—
So sang our Keats, our English nightingale.
And here, as lamps across the bridge turn pale
In London's smokeless resurrection-light,
Dark breaks to dawn. But o'er the deadly blight
Of Love deflowered and sorrow of none avail,
Which makes this man gasp and this woman quail,
Can day from darkness ever again take flight?
Ah! gave not these two hearts their mutual pledge,
Under one mantle sheltered 'neath the hedge
In gloaming courtship? And, O God! to-day
He only knows he holds her;—but what part
Can life now take ? She cries in her locked heart,—
"Leave me—I do not know you—go away!"

rossetti-day-dream.text:
The thronged boughs of the shadowy sycamore
Still bear young leaflets half the summer through;
From when the robin 'gainst the unhidden blue
Perched dark, till now, deep in the leafy core,
The embowered throstle's urgent wood-notes soar
Through summer silence. Still the leaves come new;
Yet never rosy-sheathed as those which drew
Their spiral tongues from spring-buds heretofore.
Within the branching shade of Reverie
Dreams even may spring till autumn; yet none be
Like woman's budding day-dream spirit-fann'd.
Lo, tow'rd deep skies, not deeper than her look,
She dreams; till now on her forgotten book
Drops the forgotten blossom from her hand.

rossetti-lilith.text:
Of Adam's first wife, Lilith, it is told
(The witch he loved before the gift of Eve,)
That, ere the snake's, her sweet tongue could deceive,
And her enchanted hair was the first gold.
And still she sits, young while the earth is old,
And, subtly of herself contemplative,
Draws men to watch the bright web she can weave,
Till heart and body and life are in its hold.
The rose and poppy are her flowers; for where
Is he not found, O Lilith, whom shed scent
And soft-shed kisses and soft sleep shall snare?
Lo! as that youth's eyes burned at thine, so went
Thy spell through him, and left his straight neck bent
And round his heart one strangling golden hair.
rossetti-lilith.cite: Rossetti, "Lilith" (later "Body's Beauty"), sonnet for the picture, 1868

vn-first.text: Nine times already since my birth had the heaven of light returned to the selfsame point almost, as concerns its own revolution, when first the glorious Lady of my mind was made manifest to mine eyes; even she who was called Beatrice by many who knew not wherefore. She had already been in this life for so long as that, within her time, the starry heaven had moved towards the Eastern quarter one of the twelve parts of a degree; so that she appeared to me at the beginning of her ninth year almost, and I saw her almost at the end of my ninth year. Her dress, on that day, was of a most noble colour, a subdued and goodly crimson, girdled and adorned in such sort as best suited with her very tender age. At that moment, I say most truly that the spirit of life, which hath its dwelling in the secretest chamber of the heart, began to tremble so violently that the least pulses of my body shook therewith …

vn-salutation.text:
My lady looks so gentle and so pure
When yielding salutation by the way,
That the tongue trembles and has nought to say,
And the eyes, which fain would see, may not endure.
And still, amid the praise she hears secure,
She walks with humbleness for her array;
Seeming a creature sent from Heaven to stay
On earth, and show a miracle made sure.
She is so pleasant in the eyes of men
That through the sight the inmost heart doth gain
A sweetness which needs proof to know it by:
And from between her lips there seems to move
A soothing essence that is full of love,
Saying for ever to the spirit, “Sigh!”

vn-death.text: I was still occupied with this poem, (having composed thereof only the above-written stanza,) when the Lord God of justice called my most gracious lady unto Himself, that she might be glorious under the banner of that blessed Queen Mary, whose name had always a deep reverence in the words of holy Beatrice.

vn-vanna.text: … I saw coming towards me a certain lady who was very famous for her beauty, and of whom that friend whom I have already called the first among my friends had long been enamoured. This lady’s right name was Joan; but because of her comeliness (or at least it was so imagined) she was called of many Primavera (Spring), and went by that name among them. Then looking again, I perceived that the most noble Beatrice followed after her.

dante-francesca.text:
One day we reading were for our delight
Of Launcelot, how Love did him enthral.
Alone we were and without any fear.

Full many a time our eyes together drew
That reading, and drove the colour from our faces;
But one point only was it that o’ercame us.

When as we read of the much-longed-for smile
Being by such a noble lover kissed,
This one, who ne’er from me shall be divided,

Kissed me upon the mouth all palpitating.
Galeotto was the book and he who wrote it.
That day no farther did we read therein.”

dante-gate.cite: Dante, Inferno, Canto III (the inscription over the gate of Hell)

dante-leah.text:
Youthful and beautiful in dreams methought
I saw a lady walking in a meadow,
Gathering flowers; and singing she was saying:

“Know whosoever may my name demand
That I am Leah, and go moving round
My beauteous hands to make myself a garland.

To please me at the mirror, here I deck me,
But never does my sister Rachel leave
Her looking-glass, and sitteth all day long.

To see her beauteous eyes as eager is she,
As I am to adorn me with my hands;
Her, seeing, and me, doing satisfies.”

petrarch-good-friday.text:
'Twas on the blessed morning when the sun
In pity to our Maker hid his light,
That, unawares, the captive I was won,
Lady, of your bright eyes which chain'd me quite;
That seem'd to me no time against the blows
Of love to make defence, to frame relief:
Secure and unsuspecting, thus my woes
Date their commencement from the common grief.
Love found me feeble then and fenceless all,
Open the way and easy to my heart
Through eyes, where since my sorrows ebb and flow:
But therein was, methinks, his triumph small,
On me, in that weak state, to strike his dart,
Yet hide from you so strong his very bow.

dec-ring.text: … and so they betook themselves to a little meadow, where the grass grew green and high nor there had the sun power on any side. There, feeling the waftings of a gentle breeze, they all, as their queen willed it, seated themselves in a ring on the green grass; while she bespoke them thus, "As ye see, the sun is high and the heat great, nor is aught heard save the crickets yonder among the olives; wherefore it were doubtless folly to go anywhither at this present. Here is the sojourn fair and cool, and here, as you see, are chess and tables, and each can divert himself as is most to his mind. But, an my counsel be followed in this, we shall pass away this sultry part of the day, not in gaming,—wherein the mind of one of the players must of necessity be troubled, without any great pleasure of the other or of those who look on,—but in telling stories, which, one telling, may afford diversion to all the company who hearken …

dec-fiammetta.text: Fiammetta, whose locks were curled and long and golden and fell over her white and delicate shoulders and whose soft-rounded face was all resplendent with white lilies and vermeil roses commingled, with two eyes in her head as they were those of a peregrine falcon and a dainty little mouth, the lips whereof seemed twin rubies …
dec-fiammetta.cite: Boccaccio, Decameron, end of the Fourth Day

dec-nastagio-1.text: … he saw a very fair damsel come running, naked through a thicket all thronged with underwood and briers, towards the place where he was, weeping and crying sore for mercy and all dishevelled and torn by the bushes and the brambles. At her heels ran two huge and fierce mastiffs, which followed hard upon her and ofttimes bit her cruelly, whenas they overtook her; and after them he saw come riding upon a black courser a knight arrayed in sad-coloured armour, with a very wrathful aspect and a tuck in his hand, threatening her with death in foul and fearsome words.

dec-nastagio-2.text: The latter, having made an end of his discourse, ran, tuck in hand, as he were a ravening dog, at the damsel, who, fallen on her knees and held fast by the two mastiffs, cried him mercy, and smiting her with all his might amiddleward the breast, pierced her through and through. No sooner had she received this stroke than she fell grovelling on the ground, still weeping and crying out; whereupon the knight, clapping his hand to his hunting-knife, ripped open her loins and tearing forth her heart and all that was thereabout, cast them to the two mastiffs, who devoured them incontinent, as being sore anhungred.

dec-nastagio-3.text: The time come, he seated the gentlemen and the ladies at table and so ordered it that his mistress should be placed right over against the spot where the thing should befall. Accordingly, hardly was the last dish come when the despairful outcry of the hunted damsel began to be heard of all, whereat each of the company marvelled and enquired what was to do, but none could say; whereupon all started to their feet and looking what this might be, they saw the woeful damsel and the knight and the dogs; nor was it long ere they were all there among them. Great was the clamor against both dogs and knight, and many rushed forward to succour the damsel; but the knight, bespeaking them as he had bespoken Nastagio, not only made them draw back, but filled them all with terror and amazement. Then did he as he had done before, whereat all the ladies that were there (and there were many present who had been kinswomen both to the woeful damsel and to the knight and who remembered them both of his love and of his death) wept as piteously as if they had seen this done to themselves.

dec-cymon.text: Passing therethrough, he happened (even as his fortune guided him thither) upon a little mead compassed about with very high trees, in one corner whereof was a very clear and cool spring, beside which he saw a very fair damsel asleep upon the green grass, with so thin a garment upon her body that it hid well nigh nothing of her snowy flesh. She was covered only from the waist down with a very white and light coverlet; and at her feet slept on like wise two women and a man, her servants. When Cimon espied the young lady, he halted and leaning upon his staff, fell, without saying a word, to gazing most intently upon her with the utmost admiration, no otherwise than as he had never yet seen a woman's form, whilst in his rude breast, wherein for a thousand lessonings no least impression of civil pleasance had availed to penetrate, he felt a thought awaken which intimated to his gross and material spirit that this maiden was the fairest thing that had been ever seen of any living soul.

dec-ansaldo.text: … the learned man, the night before the calends of January, so wrought by his arts in a very goodly meadow adjoining the city, that it appeared in the morning (according to the testimony of those who saw it) one of the goodliest gardens was ever seen of any, with grass and trees and fruits of every kind.

dec-bocca.text: Lips for kissing forfeit no favour; nay, they renew as the moon doth ever.
dec-bocca.cite: Boccaccio, Decameron, Day II, Story 7 (the closing proverb)

percy-rosamond.text:
When as king Henry rulde this land,
The second of that name,
Besides the queene, he dearly lovde
A faire and comely dame.

Most peerlesse was her beautye founde,
Her favour, and her face;
A sweeter creature in this worlde
Could never prince embrace.

Her crisped lockes like threads of golde
Appeard to each mans sight;
Her sparkling eyes, like Orient pearles,
Did cast a heavenlye light.

The blood within her crystal cheekes
Did such a colour drive,
As though the lillye and the rose
For mastership did strive.

Yea Rosamonde, fair Rosamonde,
Her name was called so,
To whom our queene, dame Ellinor,
Was known a deadlye foe.

The king therefore, for her defence,
Against the furious queene,
At Woodstocke builded such a bower,
The like was never seene.

Most curiously that bower was built
Of stone and timber strong,
An hundered and fifty doors
Did to this bower belong:

And they so cunninglye contriv'd
With turnings round about,
That none but with a clue of thread,
Could enter in or out.
percy-rosamond.cite: Thomas Deloney, "Fair Rosamond", in Percy's Reliques

herrick.text:
Gather ye rosebuds while ye may,
Old time is still a-flying:
And this same flower that smiles to-day
To-morrow will be dying.

The glorious lamp of heaven, the sun,
The higher he's a-getting,
The sooner will his race be run,
And nearer he's to setting.

That age is best which is the first,
When youth and blood are warmer;
But being spent, the worse, and worst
Times still succeed the former.

Then be not coy, but use your time,
And while ye may go marry:
For having lost but once your prime
You may for ever tarry.
herrick.cite: Herrick, "To the Virgins, to Make Much of Time" (1648)

browning-ruins.text:
Oh, heart! oh, blood that freezes, blood that burns!
Earth's returns
For whole centuries of folly, noise and sin!
Shut them in,
With their triumphs and their glories and the rest.
Love is best!
browning-ruins.cite: Browning, "Love Among the Ruins" (1855), last stanza
browning-ruins.note: Copied from the Wikisource transcription of the 1855 edition, whose page markup lost the line breaks; they are restored here from the poem's pattern of long and short lines.

henley-night.text:
A late lark twitters from the quiet skies;
And from the west,
Where the sun, his day’s work ended,
Lingers as in content,
There falls on the old, grey city
An influence luminous and serene,
A shining peace.

The smoke ascends
In a rosy-and-golden haze. The spires
Shine, and are changed. In the valley
Shadows rise. The lark sings on. The sun,
Closing his benediction,
Sinks, and the darkening air
Thrills with a sense of the triumphing night—
Night with her train of stars
And her great gift of sleep.

So be my passing!
My task accomplished and the long day done,
My wages taken, and in my heart
Some late lark singing,
Let me be gathered to the quiet west,
The sundown splendid and serene,
Death.

meinhold-portrait.text: Sidonia is here represented in the prime of mature beauty—a gold net is drawn over her almost golden yellow hair, and her neck, arms, and hands are profusely covered with jewels. Her bodice of bright purple is trimmed with costly fur, and the robe is of azure velvet. In her hand she carries a sort of pompadour of brown leather, of the most elegant form and finish. Her eyes and mouth are not pleasing, notwithstanding their great beauty—in the mouth, particularly, one can discover an expression of cold malignity.
meinhold-portrait.cite: Wilhelm Meinhold, Sidonia the Sorceress, Preface

segur-tree.text: The cloth was rent from the top to the bottom with a noise like thunder and Rosalie saw before her eyes a tree of marvellous beauty, with a coral trunk and leaves of emeralds. The seeming fruits which covered the tree were of precious stones of all colors—diamonds, sapphires, pearls, rubies, opals, topazes, all as large as the fruits they were intended to represent and of such brilliancy that Rosalie was completely dazzled by them.
segur-tree.cite: Comtesse de Ségur, "The Little Grey Mouse"

segur-bonnebiche.text:
Surprised, delighted, she threw her arms around the neck of Bonne-Biche, embraced Beau-Minon tenderly and said to them:

"Oh! my dear true good friends, what a debt of gratitude do I owe you for having thus watched over my childhood and developed my intellect and my heart.
segur-bonnebiche.cite: Comtesse de Ségur, "Blondine, Bonne-Biche and Beau-Minon"

segur-tortoise.text: The journey of Blondine lasted, as the Tortoise had said, six months. They were three months passing through the forest. At the end of that time she found herself on an arid plain which it required six weeks to cross. Then Blondine perceived a castle which reminded her of that of Bonne-Biche and Beau-Minon. They were a full month passing through the avenue to this castle.
segur-tortoise.cite: Comtesse de Ségur, "Blondine, Bonne-Biche and Beau-Minon"

segur-giant.text:
He had scarcely uttered these words when a part of the wall crumbled away with a terrible noise and he saw in the opening a giant, brandishing an enormous cudgel.

"You have then a great desire to pass here, my boy? What are you seeking beyond my wall?"

"I am seeking the plant of life, Master Giant, to cure my poor mother who is dying. If it is in your power and you will allow me to pass this wall, I will do anything for you that you may command."

segur-doctor.text:
In a moment he heard a noise among the plants near him and saw issue from them a little man, no taller than a hearth brush. He had a book under his arm, spectacles on his crooked little nose and wore the great black cloak of a doctor.

"What are you seeking, little one?" said the Doctor; "and how is it possible that you have gained this summit?"

"Doctor, I come from the fairy Bienfaisante, to ask the plant of life to cure my poor sick mother, who is about to die."

"All those who come from the fairy Bienfaisante," said the little Doctor, raising his hat respectfully, "are most welcome. Come, my boy, I will give you the plant you seek."

segur-rosette.text: The applause and enthusiasm for Rosette and Charmant were so overpowering that they sought refuge in the garden. They walked side by side during the rest of the evening, and talked merrily and happily over their plans for the future, if the fairy Puissante would permit them to unite the smooth current of their lives. The diamonds of Rosette sparkled with such brilliancy that the alleys where they walked and the little groves where they seated themselves, seemed illuminated by a thousand stars.

segur-ourson.text:
Violette consented willingly to pass the night in the forest. In the first place, they could not do otherwise; secondly, she was never afraid with Ourson and always thought that what he decided to do was right.

Ourson now arranged Violette's bed of moss in the best possible manner, took off his coat and in spite of her resistance spread it over her. Then, after having seen Violette's eyes close and sleep take possession of all her senses he lay at her feet and soon slept most profoundly.

livy-lucretia.text: They find Lucretia sitting in her chamber in sorrowful dejection. On the arrival of her friends the tears burst from her eyes; and to her husband, on his inquiry "whether all was right," she says, "By no means, for what can be right with a woman who has lost her honour? The traces of another man are on your bed, Collatinus. But the body only has been violated, the mind is guiltless; death shall be my witness. But give me your right hands, and your honour, that the adulterer shall not come off unpunished. It is Sextus Tarquin, who, an enemy in the guise of a guest, has borne away hence a triumph fatal to me, and to himself, if you are men." They all pledge their honour; they attempt to console her, distracted as she was in mind, by turning away the guilt from her, constrained by force, on the perpetrator of the crime; that it is the mind sins, not the body; and that where intention was wanting guilt could not be. "It is for you to see," says she, "what is due to him. As for me, though I acquit myself of guilt, from punishment I do not discharge myself; nor shall any woman survive her dishonour pleading the example of Lucretia." The knife, which she kept concealed beneath her garment, she plunges into her heart, and falling forward on the wound, she dropped down expiring.
livy-lucretia.cite: Livy, History of Rome, Book I, chapter 58

livy-virginia.text: … he draws the girl and the nurse aside to the sheds near the temple of Cloacina, which now go by the name of the new sheds: and there snatching up a knife from a butcher, "In this one way, the only one in my power, do I secure to you your liberty." He then transfixes the girl's breast, and looking back towards the tribunal, he says, "With this blood I devote thee, Appius, and thy head."
livy-virginia.cite: Livy, History of Rome, Book III, chapter 48

livy-scipio.text: The soldiers then brought to him a female captive, a grown-up virgin, of such exquisite beauty, that whichever way she walked she attracted the eyes of every body. Scipio, on making inquiries as to her country and parentage, heard, among other particulars, that she was betrothed to a young prince of the Celtiberians, named Allucius. He immediately, therefore, summoned from their abode her parents and lover, and having heard in the mean time that the latter was desperately enamoured of her, as soon as he arrived he addressed him in a more studied manner than her parents. "A young man myself," said he, "I address myself to a young man, and therefore there need be the less reserve in this conversation. As soon as your intended bride, having been captured by my soldiers, was brought into my presence, and I was informed that she was endeared to you, which her beauty rendered probable, considering that I should myself wish that my affection for my intended bride, though excessive, should meet with indulgence, could I enjoy the pleasures suited to my age, (particularly in an honourable and lawful love,) and were not my mind engrossed by public affairs, I indulge as far as I can your passion. Your mistress, while under my protection, has received as much respect as under the roof of her own parents, your father-in-law and mother-in-law. She has been kept in perfect safety for you, that she might be presented to you pure, a gift worthy of me and of you. …
livy-scipio.cite: Livy, History of Rome, Book XXVI, chapter 50

livy-scipio-gold.text: As they were so earnest in their entreaties, Scipio promised to accept it, and ordered it to be laid at his feet. Then calling Allucius to him, he said: "To the dowry which you are about to receive from your father-in-law, let these marriage presents also from me be added;" bidding him take away the gold and keep it for himself.
livy-scipio-gold.cite: Livy, History of Rome, Book XXVI, chapter 50

livy-decius.text: There it is said there appeared to both the consuls, during sleep, the same form of a man larger and more majestic than human, who said, "Of the one side a general, of the other an army was due to the dii Manes and to Mother Earth; from whichever army a general should devote the legions of the enemy and himself, in addition, that the victory would belong to that nation and that party."
livy-decius.cite: Livy, History of Rome, Book VIII, chapter 6

procopius-honorius.text: At that time they say that the Emperor Honorius in Ravenna received the message from one of the eunuchs, evidently a keeper of the poultry, that Rome had perished. And he cried out and said, "And yet it has just eaten from my hands!" For he had a very large cock, Rome by name; and the eunuch comprehending his words said that it was the city of Rome which had perished at the hands of Alaric, and the emperor with a sigh of relief answered quickly: "But I, my good fellow, thought that my fowl Rome had perished."
procopius-honorius.cite: Procopius, History of the Wars, III.ii.25–26

froissart-calais.text: After a short time the most wealthy citizen of the town, by name Eustace de St. Pierre, rose up and said, “Gentlemen, both high and low, it would be a very great pity to suffer so many people to die through famine, if any means could be found to prevent it; and it would be highly meritorious in the eyes of our Saviour, if such misery could be averted. I have such faith and trust in finding grace before God, if I die to save my townsmen, that I name myself as first of the six.” When Eustace had done speaking, they all rose up and almost worshipped him: many cast themselves at his feet with tears and groans. Another citizen, very rich and respected, rose up, and said he would be the second to his companion Eustace; his name was John Daire. After him, James Wisant, who was very rich in merchandise and lands, offered himself as companion to his two cousins; as did Peter Wisant his brother. Two others then named themselves, which completed the number demanded by the King of England.

r3-princes.text:
“O, thus,” quoth Dighton, “lay the gentle babes;”
“Thus, thus,” quoth Forrest, “girdling one another
Within their alabaster innocent arms.
Their lips were four red roses on a stalk,
And in their summer beauty kissed each other.
A book of prayers on their pillow lay,
Which once,” quoth Forrest, “almost changed my mind.

vasari-cimabue.text: He next painted a picture of Our Lady for the church of S. Maria Novella, where it hangs high up between the chapel of the Rucellai and that of the Bardi of Vernio. The figure was of a larger size than any which had been executed up to that time, and the angels about it show that, although he still had the Byzantine style, he was making some progress towards the lineaments and methods of modern times. The people of that day, who had never seen anything better, considered this work so marvellous, that they carried it to the church from Cimabue's house in a stately procession with great rejoicing and blowing of trumpets, while Cimabue himself was highly rewarded and honoured. It is reported, and some records of the old painters relate that while Cimabue was painting this picture in some gardens near the gate of S. Piero, the old king Charles of Anjou passed through Florence. Among the many entertainments prepared for him by the men of the city, they brought him to see the picture of Cimabue. As it had not then been seen by anyone, all the men and women of Florence flocked thither in a crowd, with the greatest rejoicings, so that those who lived in the neighbourhood called the place Borgo Allegri (Joyful Quarter), because of the rejoicing there.
vasari-cimabue.cite: Vasari, Lives of the Painters, "Life of Cimabue"
vasari-cimabue.note: Two misprints in the transcription are corrected: "be" for "he", and a stray comma.

michelangelo-the-separation-of-light-fro.subject: creation
michelangelo-the-separation-of-light-fro.scene: The first day of Creation, the last of the nine ceiling scenes that Michelangelo painted, directly over the altar: God alone, twisting upward as he parts the light from the dark.

michelangelo-the-creation-of-the-sun-moo.subject: creation
michelangelo-the-creation-of-the-sun-moo.scene: Two moments in one panel: on the right God, arms outstretched, sets the sun and moon in the sky; on the left he is seen from behind, flying off to bring forth the plants.

michelangelo-the-creation-of-adam.webp.subject: adam-and-eve
michelangelo-the-creation-of-adam.webp.scene: God, borne by angels, reaches out to give life to Adam, who lies on the bare earth with his hand barely lifted. The gap between the two fingers is the moment before the spark of life passes.

michelangelo-the-creation-of-eve.webp.subject: adam-and-eve
michelangelo-the-creation-of-eve.webp.scene: Adam lies asleep against a dead tree as Eve rises from his side at a gesture from God, her hands joined in thanks.

michelangelo-the-fall-and-expulsion-from.subject: adam-and-eve
michelangelo-the-fall-and-expulsion-from.scene: Two scenes divided by the tree: on the left Adam and Eve take the fruit from the serpent, a woman to the waist and a snake below; on the right an angel with a sword drives them, aged and ashamed, out of Eden.

rodin-eve.webp.subject: adam-and-eve
rodin-eve.webp.scene: Rodin made Eve for the Gates of Hell, his great doorway of figures from Dante. She stands after the Fall, turning away and covering herself, ashamed.

rodin-hand-of-god.webp.subject: adam-and-eve
rodin-hand-of-god.webp.scene: A huge right hand rises from the rough marble holding a man and woman, still half unformed, curled together in its palm: God in the act of making Adam and Eve.

michelangelo-the-deluge.webp.subject: noah
michelangelo-the-deluge.webp.scene: The waters rise over the last high ground. People crowd onto a rock carrying what they can, a boat capsizes under those trying to climb aboard, and the ark floats closed in the distance.

michelangelo-the-sacrifice-of-noah.webp.subject: noah
michelangelo-the-sacrifice-of-noah.webp.scene: After the flood Noah and his family give thanks with a burnt offering; his sons bring the ram and kindle the fire while his wife and daughters-in-law look on.

michelangelo-the-drunkenness-of-noah.web.subject: noah
michelangelo-the-drunkenness-of-noah.web.scene: Noah lies asleep and uncovered after drinking the wine of his vineyard, and his sons come to cover him. In the background he works the soil.

turner-the-evening-of-the-deluge.webp.subject: noah
turner-the-evening-of-the-deluge.webp.scene: Turner paints the eve of the flood: a darkening sky over a crowd going about its business, and in the far distance the animals moving in pairs towards the ark.

millais-the-return-of-the-dove-to-the-ar.subject: noah
millais-the-return-of-the-dove-to-the-ar.scene: Inside the dim ark two young women, perhaps Noah's daughters-in-law, hold the dove that has just flown back with an olive branch, the first sign that the flood is going down.

rubens-the-meeting-of-abraham-and-melchi.subject: abraham
rubens-the-meeting-of-abraham-and-melchi.scene: Melchizedek, king and priest, comes down the steps with bread and wine to meet Abraham, who arrives in armour after rescuing Lot. Christians read the bread and wine as a foreshadowing of the Eucharist; Rubens designed it for a tapestry series on that theme.

caravaggio-the-sacrifice-of-isaac.webp.subject: abraham
caravaggio-the-sacrifice-of-isaac.webp.scene: Abraham pins his son's head to the stone with the knife in his hand as the angel seizes his arm and points to the ram. Isaac cries out, looking straight at us.

brown-the-coat-of-many-colours.webp.subject: joseph
brown-the-coat-of-many-colours.webp.scene: Joseph's brothers bring Jacob the bloodstained coat. The old man starts back in grief; the youngest son, Benjamin, clings to his knee, and one of the brothers watches to see how the lie is taken.

botticelli-the-trials-of-moses.webp.subject: moses
botticelli-the-trials-of-moses.webp.scene: Botticelli's Sistine Chapel fresco tells several episodes at once: Moses kills the Egyptian, flees, drives off the shepherds and waters the flocks of Jethro's daughters, takes off his shoes before the burning bush, and leads the Israelites out of Egypt.

botticelli-the-punishment-of-korah.webp.subject: moses
botticelli-the-punishment-of-korah.webp.scene: Korah and his followers challenged the authority of Moses and Aaron by offering incense themselves. Botticelli shows Moses calling down judgement and the earth opening to swallow them, with the Arch of Constantine behind as a warning to those who defy the Pope.

hunt-the-scapegoat.webp.subject: scapegoat
hunt-the-scapegoat.webp.scene: Hunt painted the goat on the salt shore of the Dead Sea itself, working there in 1854. It stands near death in the poisoned landscape with a red cloth bound round its horns, the sign of the sins laid on it.

caravaggio-david-and-goliath.webp.subject: david
caravaggio-david-and-goliath.webp.scene: David kneels on the fallen giant's back, binding the hair of the severed head to carry it off.

caravaggio-david-with-the-head-of-goliat.subject: david
caravaggio-david-with-the-head-of-goliat.scene: David, sword on his shoulder, holds up the head of Goliath and looks out at us.

caravaggio-david-with-the-head-of-goliat.subject: david
caravaggio-david-with-the-head-of-goliat.scene: David holds out Goliath's head with an expression closer to pity than triumph. The head is thought to be a self-portrait of Caravaggio, painted when he was a fugitive under sentence of death.

leighton-david.webp.subject: david
leighton-david.webp.scene: King David, in his moment of deepest doubt after the death of his rebellious son Absalom, sits against a wall looking over the mountains as two white doves fly into the gold evening sky. Leighton made the psalm part of the title.

leighton-jonathans-token-to-david.webp.subject: david
leighton-jonathans-token-to-david.webp.scene: Jonathan stands with his bow, ready to shoot the arrows that will tell David, hidden nearby, whether it is safe to return to Saul's court.

rubens-the-meeting-of-david-and-abigail..subject: david
rubens-the-meeting-of-david-and-abigail..scene: Abigail kneels before David and his armed men with gifts of food to turn him from vengeance on her husband Nabal.

brown-elijah-and-the-widows-son.webp.subject: elijah
brown-elijah-and-the-widows-son.webp.scene: Elijah brings the child, alive again and still in his grave clothes, down the outside stair to his mother.

leighton-elijah-in-the-wilderness.webp.subject: elijah
leighton-elijah-in-the-wilderness.webp.scene: The prophet lies exhausted in the desert, and an angel comes down to him with bread and a cruse of water.

gentileschi-esther-before-ahasuerus.webp.subject: esther
gentileschi-esther-before-ahasuerus.webp.scene: Esther faints before the king, held by her maids, as Ahasuerus starts from his throne. Gentileschi follows the Greek additions to the story, in which the queen collapses at his look.

rubens-daniel-in-the-lions-den.webp.subject: daniel
rubens-daniel-in-the-lions-den.webp.scene: Daniel prays in the den with nine lions around him, life-size, painted by Rubens from lions in a menagerie.

michelangelo-the-prophet-isaiah.webp.subject: prophets
michelangelo-the-prophet-isaiah.webp.scene: Isaiah turns from his book as if called by the child angel at his shoulder.

michelangelo-the-prophet-joel-fresco.web.subject: prophets
michelangelo-the-prophet-joel-fresco.web.scene: Joel, an old man, reads a scroll intently.

michelangelo-the-prophet-jonah.webp.subject: prophets
michelangelo-the-prophet-jonah.webp.scene: Jonah leans back over the altar wall beside the great fish that swallowed him and the gourd that shaded him. He was read as a sign of Christ, three days in the belly of the fish as Christ was three days in the tomb.

michelangelo-the-prophet-ezekiel-fresco..subject: prophets
michelangelo-the-prophet-ezekiel-fresco..scene: Ezekiel turns sharply with a scroll in his hand, as if answering a voice.

michelangelo-the-prophet-daniel.webp.subject: prophets
michelangelo-the-prophet-daniel.webp.scene: Daniel copies from a huge book held up by a child.

michelangelo-study-for-the-nude-youth-ov.subject: prophets
michelangelo-study-for-the-nude-youth-ov.scene: A red chalk study for one of the nude youths, the ignudi, who sit above the prophet Daniel on the ceiling.

subject: prophets
tree-of-jesse
saxon-prophet-isaiah.webp.scene: A carved and painted prophet from a church in Saxony, holding the scroll of his prophecy.

saxon-prophet-daniel.webp.subject: prophets
saxon-prophet-daniel.webp.scene: A carved and painted figure, thought to be Daniel, from the same Saxon church furnishings as the Isaiah. The identification is the Met's, with a question mark.
saxon-prophet-daniel.webp.uncertain: The Met identifies the figure as Daniel only tentatively.

saxon-prophet-king.webp.subject: tree-of-jesse
saxon-prophet-king.webp.scene: One of the kings of Israel from a stained-glass Tree of Jesse window: Christ's ancestors seated among the branches.

michelangelo-the-delphic-sibyl-fresco.we.subject: sibyls
michelangelo-the-delphic-sibyl-fresco.we.scene: The sibyl of Apollo's oracle at Delphi turns from her scroll, eyes wide.

michelangelo-the-libyan-sibyl.webp.subject: sibyls
michelangelo-the-libyan-sibyl.webp.scene: The Libyan sibyl twists to lift down, or put away, her great book of oracles.

michelangelo-studies-for-the-libyan-siby.subject: sibyls
michelangelo-studies-for-the-libyan-siby.scene: Red chalk studies from a male model for the twisting pose of the Libyan sibyl, with separate studies of her hand, foot and face.

michelangelo-the-erythraean-sibyl.webp.subject: sibyls
michelangelo-the-erythraean-sibyl.webp.scene: The sibyl of Erythrae turns the pages of her book while a child lights the lamp above.

michelangelo-the-persian-sibyl-fresco.we.subject: sibyls
michelangelo-the-persian-sibyl-fresco.we.scene: The aged Persian sibyl, hunched in profile, holds her book close to her eyes.

botticelli-the-return-of-judith-to-bethu.subject: judith
botticelli-the-return-of-judith-to-bethu.scene: Judith walks home through the hills carrying the sword, her maid following with the head of Holofernes in a basket on her own head.

botticelli-the-discovery-of-the-body-of-.subject: judith
botticelli-the-discovery-of-the-body-of-.scene: The companion panel: in the Assyrian camp Holofernes's officers draw back the curtain of his tent and find his headless body.

botticelli-judith-with-the-head-of-holof.subject: judith
botticelli-judith-with-the-head-of-holof.scene: A small late panel of Judith leaving the tent with the head in her hand.

caravaggio-judith-beheading-holofernes.w.subject: judith
caravaggio-judith-beheading-holofernes.w.scene: Judith draws the sword through Holofernes's neck at arm's length while her old maid waits with the bag.

gentileschi-judith-slaying-holofernes.we.subject: judith
gentileschi-judith-slaying-holofernes.we.scene: Judith and her maid pin Holofernes down together as Judith cuts. Gentileschi painted the subject several times; this is the Uffizi version.

gentileschi-judith-and-her-maidservant.w.subject: judith
gentileschi-judith-and-her-maidservant.w.scene: Judith and her maid, the head in a basket, freeze by candlelight in the tent as if they have heard someone coming.

gentileschi-susanna-and-the-elders.webp.subject: susanna
gentileschi-susanna-and-the-elders.webp.scene: Gentileschi's first known painting, made at seventeen: Susanna recoils from the two elders leaning over the wall behind her.

bellini-madonna-and-child.webp.subject: madonna
bellini-madonna-and-child.webp.scene: Mary holds the Child before a landscape, behind a stone ledge that separates the holy figures from us.

bellini-madonna-and-child-in-a-landscape.subject: madonna
bellini-madonna-and-child-in-a-landscape.scene: Mary sits in the open countryside with the Child on her lap.

botticelli-madonna-and-child.webp.subject: madonna
botticelli-madonna-and-child.webp.scene: An early Madonna, close to the style of Botticelli's teacher Filippo Lippi.

botticelli-the-virgin-adoring-the-child..subject: madonna
botticelli-the-virgin-adoring-the-child..scene: Mary kneels in adoration before the Child lying on the ground in a garden enclosed by roses; the enclosed garden was a symbol of her purity.

botticelli-madonna-and-child-with-two-an.subject: madonna
botticelli-madonna-and-child-with-two-an.scene: An early work: two young angels hold the Child up to his mother.

botticelli-the-sant-ambrogio-altarpiece..subject: madonna
botticelli-the-sant-ambrogio-altarpiece..scene: The Virgin and Child enthroned among saints, among them Cosmas and Damian, the patron saints of the Medici, kneeling in front.

botticelli-madonna-and-child-with-singin.subject: madonna
botticelli-madonna-and-child-with-singin.scene: A round picture: angels crowd round the Virgin holding tall white lilies, the flower of her purity, and singing.

botticelli-virgin-and-child-with-an-ange.subject: madonna
botticelli-virgin-and-child-with-an-ange.scene: An angel supports the Child at his mother's side.

botticelli-madonna-of-the-book.webp.subject: madonna
botticelli-madonna-of-the-book.webp.scene: Mary has been reading her Book of Hours with the Child on her lap; he holds three golden nails and wears the crown of thorns like a bracelet on his wrist, signs of the Passion to come.

botticelli-the-bardi-madonna.webp.subject: madonna
botticelli-the-bardi-madonna.webp.scene: Made for the chapel of the Bardi family in Santo Spirito, Florence: the Virgin enthroned in a bower of greenery, with John the Baptist and John the Evangelist.

botticelli-the-virgin-adoring-the-sleepi.subject: madonna
botticelli-the-virgin-adoring-the-sleepi.scene: Mary kneels in a garden of roses before the Child asleep on a cushion.

botticelli-madonna-of-the-pomegranate.we.subject: madonna
botticelli-madonna-of-the-pomegranate.we.scene: A round picture: the Child holds a pomegranate, whose many seeds in one fruit stood for the church and whose red juice for the Passion, and Mary is ringed by six angels.

botticelli-virgin-and-child-with-the-you.subject: madonna
botticelli-virgin-and-child-with-the-you.scene: The Christ Child leans from his mother's arms to embrace his cousin John.

botticelli-madonna-del-padiglione.webp.subject: madonna
botticelli-madonna-del-padiglione.webp.scene: Angels draw back the curtains of a canopy, or pavilion, to reveal the Virgin nursing the Child.

raphael-the-small-cowper-madonna.webp.subject: madonna
raphael-the-small-cowper-madonna.webp.scene: Painted in Florence when Raphael was about twenty-two. The church on the hill behind may be San Bernardino near Urbino, his home town.

raphael-the-niccolini-cowper-madonna.web.subject: madonna
raphael-the-niccolini-cowper-madonna.web.scene: The Child twists in his mother's lap and clutches at the neckline of her dress.

raphael-the-alba-madonna.webp.subject: madonna
raphael-the-alba-madonna.webp.scene: A round picture: Mary sits on the ground in a wide landscape, and the Child takes from the young John the Baptist a little cross of reeds, accepting his fate. It belonged to the Dukes of Alba and was sold by the Soviet government to Andrew Mellon in 1931.

leonardo-da-vinci-madonna-of-the-carnati.subject: madonna
leonardo-da-vinci-madonna-of-the-carnati.scene: The Child reaches for a red carnation that his mother holds, the flower that stood for the Passion.

leonardo-da-vinci-benois-madonna.webp.subject: madonna
leonardo-da-vinci-benois-madonna.webp.scene: A young, laughing Mary shows the Child a flower with four petals, a cross, which he studies intently.

subject: madonna
holy-family
leonardo-da-vinci-virgin-of-the-rocks.we.scene: In a dark grotto the Virgin presents the infant John the Baptist, kneeling, to the Child, who blesses him, while an angel points. The meeting comes from a legend that the Holy Family met John in the desert on the way to Egypt. Leonardo painted the subject twice; this is the earlier version, in the Louvre.

leonardo-da-vinci-the-virgin-and-child-w.subject: saint-anne
leonardo-da-vinci-the-virgin-and-child-w.scene: Mary sits on her mother's lap and leans down to draw the Child away from a lamb, the sign of his sacrifice, which he holds on to. Leonardo kept the painting with him until his death.

leonardo-da-vinci-the-virgin-and-child-w.subject: saint-anne
leonardo-da-vinci-the-virgin-and-child-w.scene: The Burlington House Cartoon, a full-size drawing: Mary on Saint Anne's lap holds the Child, who blesses the young John; Anne points upward to heaven.

leonardo-da-vinci-the-head-of-the-virgin.subject: saint-anne
leonardo-da-vinci-the-head-of-the-virgin.scene: A study of the Virgin's head, bowed and smiling, for the painting of the Virgin and Child with Saint Anne.

michelangelo-manchester-madonna.webp.subject: madonna
michelangelo-manchester-madonna.webp.scene: Unfinished: the Virgin draws her robe over her breast as the Child reaches for the book in her lap, the young John beside him, and angels read from a scroll.

subject: holy-family
saint-anne
el-greco-the-holy-family-with-saint-anne.scene: Mary lifts a veil from the sleeping Child, Saint Anne and Joseph look on, and the infant John puts a finger to his lips for silence.
el-greco-the-holy-family-with-saint-anne.uncertain: The gestures are from memory of the picture; check them against it.

stella-madonna.webp.subject: madonna
stella-madonna.webp.scene: Joseph Stella, an Italian-born American modernist, painted a Madonna in the manner of the early Italian masters, ringed with flowers.
stella-madonna.webp.uncertain: Described from the title and Stella's other work of the time; check against the picture.

stella-purissima.webp.subject: madonna
stella-purissima.webp.scene: Purissima, "most pure", is one of the titles of the Virgin. Stella painted a huge, hieratic woman surrounded by flowers and fruit.
stella-purissima.webp.uncertain: Described from the title; check against the picture.

botticelli-the-cestello-annunciation.web.subject: annunciation
botticelli-the-cestello-annunciation.web.scene: Gabriel has just knelt and Mary sways back from him, her hand raised.

botticelli-the-annunciation-glasgow.webp.subject: annunciation
botticelli-the-annunciation-glasgow.webp.scene: A small panel set in a long, bare loggia, with the angel arriving in mid-flight.

botticelli-the-annunciation.webp.subject: annunciation
botticelli-the-annunciation.webp.scene: A small Annunciation in the Met, with the angel kneeling in a deep, empty hall.

leonardo-da-vinci-annunciation.webp.subject: annunciation
leonardo-da-vinci-annunciation.webp.scene: Leonardo's early Annunciation, painted in Verrocchio's workshop: Gabriel kneels on a lawn before a garden wall, and Mary raises her hand from her book.

rossetti-ecce-ancilla-domini.webp.subject: annunciation
rossetti-ecce-ancilla-domini.webp.scene: Rossetti's Annunciation, painted almost all in white: a frightened girl shrinks against the wall of her bed as the angel holds out a lily. The title is the Latin of Mary's answer. His sister Christina sat for Mary.

subject: madonna
magnificat
botticelli-madonna-of-the-magnificat.web.scene: Mary writes the Magnificat in a book held by angels, guiding the Child's hand, which rests on a pomegranate. Two angels hold a crown over her.

botticelli-the-mystical-nativity.webp.subject: nativity
botticelli-the-mystical-nativity.webp.scene: Painted in 1500–01 in the troubled Florence after Savonarola's death. Angels dance in a ring above the stable, angels embrace men below, and devils flee into the rocks. A Greek inscription by Botticelli at the top speaks of the troubles of Italy and of the devil chained, from the Book of Revelation.

hughes-the-nativity.webp.subject: nativity
hughes-the-nativity.webp.scene: Small angels kneel round the manger in the night, one playing music, in Arthur Hughes's Nativity.

caravaggio-adoration-of-the-shepherds.we.subject: nativity
caravaggio-adoration-of-the-shepherds.we.scene: Painted in Messina in Caravaggio's last years: the shepherds kneel by Mary, who lies on the straw of a bare stable with the Child against her face.

subject: nativity
caravaggio-nativity-with-saint-francis-a.scene: The Nativity with two saints who were not there: Francis, who made the first Christmas crib, and Lawrence with his gridiron. The painting was stolen from an oratory in Palermo in 1969 and has never been found.

botticelli-the-adoration-of-the-magi.web.subject: magi
botticelli-the-adoration-of-the-magi.web.scene: An Adoration in Washington: the kings and their train fill a ruined classical building, the old world from whose ruins the new faith grows.

botticelli-the-adoration-of-the-magi-flo.subject: magi
botticelli-the-adoration-of-the-magi-flo.scene: Botticelli's best-known Adoration, made for a banker's chapel. The kings are portraits of the Medici, Cosimo kneeling at the Child's feet, and the young man in yellow at the right edge, looking at us, is thought to be Botticelli himself.

botticelli-the-adoration-of-the-magi-lon.subject: magi
botticelli-the-adoration-of-the-magi-lon.scene: An early Adoration, a long panel with crowds of riders and horses arriving from both sides.

leonardo-da-vinci-adoration-of-the-magi..subject: magi
leonardo-da-vinci-adoration-of-the-magi..scene: Leonardo left this Adoration unfinished when he moved to Milan in 1482: a whirl of figures round the Virgin under a tree, with battling horsemen among the ruins behind.

burne-jones-the-star-of-bethlehem.webp.subject: magi
burne-jones-the-star-of-bethlehem.webp.scene: A huge watercolour: the three kings arrive at a wattle shelter in a wood, where Mary sits with the Child and an angel holds up the star.

rembrandt-van-rijn-the-circumcision.webp.subject: circumcision
rembrandt-van-rijn-the-circumcision.webp.scene: One of Rembrandt's last paintings: the ceremony in a stable by lantern light, Mary holding the child and a priest bending to the task.

caravaggio-rest-on-the-flight-into-egypt.subject: flight-into-egypt
caravaggio-rest-on-the-flight-into-egypt.scene: On the road to Egypt the Virgin sleeps with the Child in her arms while an angel plays the violin from music that Joseph holds up for him.

hunt-the-triumph-of-the-innocents.webp.subject: flight-into-egypt
hunt-the-triumph-of-the-innocents.webp.scene: The Holy Family flees by night, and round them float the spirits of the children killed by Herod, crowned with flowers and rejoicing.

saxon-massacre-of-the-innocents.webp.subject: flight-into-egypt
saxon-massacre-of-the-innocents.webp.scene: An enamel plaque in which Herod's soldiers kill the children of Bethlehem.

hunt-the-finding-of-the-saviour-in-the-t.subject: finding-in-temple
hunt-the-finding-of-the-saviour-in-the-t.scene: Mary embraces the boy Jesus, who turns from the rabbis of the Temple. Hunt worked on it in Jerusalem for six years, using Jewish men there as models.

millais-christ-in-the-house-of-his-paren.subject: holy-family
millais-christ-in-the-house-of-his-paren.scene: In Joseph's workshop the boy Jesus has cut his hand on a nail and his mother kneels to comfort him, a foreshadowing of the Crucifixion; the young John brings a bowl of water. Charles Dickens attacked it as ugly and irreverent.

subject: madonna
saint-anne
caravaggio-madonna-and-child-with-saint-.scene: Mary and the Child together crush the head of the serpent under their feet, while Saint Anne watches. Painted for the papal grooms' altar in Saint Peter's, it was soon taken down.

leonardo-da-vinci-the-baptism-of-christ..subject: baptism
leonardo-da-vinci-the-baptism-of-christ..scene: Begun by Andrea del Verrocchio in about 1470. Vasari says the young Leonardo painted the angel on the left, so well that his master gave up painting.

caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist-youth-.subject: john-the-baptist
caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist-youth-.scene: Caravaggio shows John as a laughing boy with his arm round a ram, in place of the usual lamb.

caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist-in-the.subject: john-the-baptist
caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist-in-the.scene: A brooding young John sits in the wilderness with his reed cross and red cloak.

caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist-corsin.subject: john-the-baptist
caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist-corsin.scene: Another young John in the wilderness, painted at about the same time.

caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist.webp.subject: john-the-baptist
caravaggio-saint-john-the-baptist.webp.scene: One of the last paintings Caravaggio made, perhaps carried with him on his final journey in 1610: the young John lying with a ram.

leonardo-da-vinci-saint-john-the-baptist.subject: john-the-baptist
leonardo-da-vinci-saint-john-the-baptist.scene: John smiles out of the darkness and points upward to heaven, to the one who comes after him.

anglo-saxon-pectoral-with-christ-and-the.subject: john-the-baptist
anglo-saxon-pectoral-with-christ-and-the.scene: A small ivory carved with Christ and the Lamb of God, the figure that John's words gave to the church.

caravaggio-the-beheading-of-saint-john-t.subject: salome
caravaggio-the-beheading-of-saint-john-t.scene: Caravaggio's largest painting, for the knights of Malta, and the only one he signed, in the blood flowing from John's neck. The executioner reaches for his knife while Salome holds out the dish.

caravaggio-salome-with-the-head-of-john-.subject: salome
caravaggio-salome-with-the-head-of-john-.scene: Salome turns her face away as the executioner lays the head on her dish.

caravaggio-salome-with-the-head-of-john-.subject: salome
caravaggio-salome-with-the-head-of-john-.scene: Salome, an old woman and the executioner gather round the head on the platter, in Caravaggio's London version.

botticelli-the-temptations-of-christ.web.subject: temptation
botticelli-the-temptations-of-christ.web.scene: Botticelli's Sistine fresco shows the three temptations in the background, with the devil disguised as a hermit, and in front a priest at the Temple offering the sacrifice of a leper healed.

caravaggio-the-calling-of-saint-matthew..subject: calling-of-apostles
caravaggio-the-calling-of-saint-matthew..scene: Christ, hardly seen in the shadow behind Peter, points into a counting-room, and a shaft of light falls on the tax collectors. Which of them is Matthew, the bearded man pointing at himself or the young man still counting coins, is still argued.

caravaggio-the-calling-of-saints-peter-a.subject: calling-of-apostles
caravaggio-the-calling-of-saints-peter-a.scene: Christ calls the fisherman brothers, Andrew holding a fish.

el-greco-christ-cleansing-the-temple.web.subject: cleansing-temple
el-greco-christ-cleansing-the-temple.web.scene: Christ raises the whip against the traders in a classical courtyard, those on the left recoiling, the apostles on the right calm.

subject: martha-and-mary
mary-magdalene
caravaggio-martha-and-mary-magdalene.web.scene: Martha leans out of the dark, counting off arguments on her fingers, as her sister Mary, in a rich dress, holds a mirror and the orange blossom of a bride: the moment of her conversion.

caravaggio-penitent-magdalene.webp.subject: mary-magdalene
caravaggio-penitent-magdalene.webp.scene: A young woman sits on a low chair with her head bowed and her pearls and jewels thrown on the floor beside her.

caravaggio-the-raising-of-lazarus.webp.subject: lazarus
caravaggio-the-raising-of-lazarus.webp.scene: Painted in Messina: the stiff body, held up by the men who have opened the grave, comes back to life as Christ points.

caravaggio-the-seven-works-of-mercy.webp.subject: works-of-mercy
caravaggio-the-seven-works-of-mercy.webp.scene: Caravaggio set all seven works in one Naples street at night: a woman feeds an old prisoner from her breast, Saint Martin shares his cloak, a corpse is carried out, and the Madonna and Child look down with two angels.

leonardo-da-vinci-the-last-supper.webp.subject: last-supper
leonardo-da-vinci-the-last-supper.webp.scene: The moment after Christ has said that one of them will betray him. The apostles break into four groups of three in their alarm; Judas, clutching the bag of silver, draws back into shadow. Leonardo painted it on the refectory wall of Santa Maria delle Grazie in Milan in an oil technique that began to flake within his lifetime.

caravaggio-the-taking-of-christ.webp.subject: passion
caravaggio-the-taking-of-christ.webp.scene: Judas kisses Christ as the soldiers seize him. The man holding the lantern on the right is thought to be Caravaggio. The painting was lost for two centuries and found in 1990 in a Jesuit house in Dublin.

caravaggio-the-denial-of-saint-peter.web.subject: passion
caravaggio-the-denial-of-saint-peter.web.scene: A soldier and a servant girl accuse Peter by the fire; he points to himself as if to deny it.

caravaggio-the-flagellation-of-christ.we.subject: passion
caravaggio-the-flagellation-of-christ.we.scene: Three tormentors bind Christ to the column in the dark.

caravaggio-christ-at-the-column.webp.subject: passion
caravaggio-christ-at-the-column.webp.scene: Christ is bound to the column as the scourging begins.

caravaggio-the-crowning-with-thorns.webp.subject: passion
caravaggio-the-crowning-with-thorns.webp.scene: Soldiers press the crown of thorns onto Christ's head with staves.

caravaggio-ecce-homo.webp.subject: passion
caravaggio-ecce-homo.webp.scene: Pilate shows the scourged Christ to the crowd, and a soldier draws the purple robe from his shoulders.

botticelli-mystic-crucifixion.webp.subject: crucifixion
botticelli-mystic-crucifixion.webp.scene: A late, visionary picture from the years of Savonarola: Mary Magdalene clings to the cross, an angel whips a fox, and Florence stands behind under a sky of storm and fire.

saxon-crucifix.webp.subject: crucifixion
saxon-crucifix.webp.scene: A gilt-bronze crucifix figure of the twelfth century, the crucified Christ shown calm and upright as king.

botticelli-lamentation-over-the-dead-chr.subject: entombment
botticelli-lamentation-over-the-dead-chr.scene: Mary swoons over her dead son in the arms of John, while the Magdalene holds his feet and another Mary his head.

caravaggio-the-entombment-of-christ.webp.subject: entombment
caravaggio-the-entombment-of-christ.webp.scene: Nicodemus and John lower Christ's body onto the stone of anointing; the three Marys mourn behind.

michelangelo-the-entombment.webp.subject: entombment
michelangelo-the-entombment.webp.scene: Unfinished: the dead Christ is carried upright to the tomb. Mary's figure, in the lower right, was never painted.

caravaggio-the-supper-at-emmaus.webp.subject: emmaus
caravaggio-the-supper-at-emmaus.webp.scene: The beardless Christ blesses the bread and the two disciples start up in recognition, one flinging out his arms. A basket of fruit teeters on the table edge.

caravaggio-supper-at-emmaus-milan.webp.subject: emmaus
caravaggio-supper-at-emmaus-milan.webp.scene: A quieter, darker version painted five years later, when Caravaggio was on the run after killing a man.

caravaggio-the-incredulity-of-saint-thom.subject: doubting-thomas
caravaggio-the-incredulity-of-saint-thom.scene: Christ guides Thomas's finger into the wound in his side, and two other apostles lean in to look.

saxon-saint-thomas.webp.subject: doubting-thomas
saxon-saint-thomas.webp.scene: An enamel plaque of the apostle Thomas.

caravaggio-the-conversion-of-saint-paul..subject: conversion-of-paul
caravaggio-the-conversion-of-saint-paul..scene: Saul lies on his back under his horse, arms raised to the light that has blinded him; the groom sees nothing.

caravaggio-conversion-on-the-way-to-dama.subject: conversion-of-paul
caravaggio-conversion-on-the-way-to-dama.scene: The first version, crowded and stormy, with Christ held by an angel reaching down to Saul.

michelangelo-the-conversion-of-saul.webp.subject: conversion-of-paul
michelangelo-the-conversion-of-saul.webp.scene: Painted in the Pauline Chapel of the Vatican when Michelangelo was nearly seventy: Christ plunges from heaven, and the old Saul lies stunned among his scattering soldiers.

rembrandt-van-rijn-the-apostle-paul.webp.subject: apostle-paul
rembrandt-van-rijn-the-apostle-paul.webp.scene: Paul sits writing at a table, the hilt of the sword of his martyrdom beside him.

titian-saint-john-the-evangelist-on-patm.subject: john-evangelist
titian-saint-john-the-evangelist-on-patm.scene: A ceiling painting, seen from below: John on Patmos flings up his arms at the vision of God, his eagle beside him.

saxon-saint-john-at-his-desk.webp.subject: john-evangelist
saxon-saint-john-at-his-desk.webp.scene: A painted wooden figure of John writing his Gospel.

hunt-the-light-of-the-world.webp.subject: revelation
hunt-the-light-of-the-world.webp.scene: Christ, crowned with thorns and carrying a lantern, knocks at an overgrown door that has no handle on the outside: it can only be opened from within. Hunt painted the night scene by moonlight in an orchard.

leighton-and-the-sea-gave-up-the-dead-wh.subject: revelation
leighton-and-the-sea-gave-up-the-dead-wh.scene: Made as a design for Saint Paul's Cathedral: a man rises from the sea at the last judgement, holding his wife and child.

hunt-the-awakening-conscience.webp.subject: awakening-conscience
hunt-the-awakening-conscience.webp.scene: The woman starts up from her lover's lap with a look of sudden understanding; the cat under the table toying with a bird stands for her plight.

burne-jones-hope.webp.subject: hope
burne-jones-hope.webp.scene: Hope stands in a cell, her ankles chained, reaching up with a branch of apple blossom toward the open window.

edward-robert-hughes-wings-of-the-mornin.subject: wings-of-the-morning
edward-robert-hughes-wings-of-the-mornin.scene: A winged figure soars over the sea at dawn.

brown-work.webp.subject: work
brown-work.webp.scene: The navvies at the centre, the idle and the outcast around them. The verses are carved on the frame of the Manchester picture.

raphael-saint-george-and-the-dragon.webp.subject: saint-george
raphael-saint-george-and-the-dragon.webp.scene: A small panel: George, on a white horse, drives his lance into the dragon as the princess prays at the edge of the wood. He wears the Garter on his leg; the picture may have been a gift for Henry VII of England.

botticelli-saint-sebastian.webp.subject: saint-sebastian
botticelli-saint-sebastian.webp.scene: Sebastian stands calm and unhurt-looking, tied to a tree, the arrows already in him, above a wide landscape. Painted in 1474 for the church of Santa Maria Maggiore in Florence.

corot-saint-sebastian-succored-by-the-ho.subject: saint-sebastian
corot-saint-sebastian-succored-by-the-ho.scene: Late in life Corot painted the sequel to the martyrdom: in a darkening wood the holy women draw the arrows from Sebastian's body, while two angels come down with a palm and a crown.

bellini-saint-jerome-reading.webp.subject: saint-jerome
bellini-saint-jerome-reading.webp.scene: Jerome sits reading on a rock in the wilderness, with a walled town in the distance.

leonardo-da-vinci-saint-jerome-in-the-wi.subject: saint-jerome
leonardo-da-vinci-saint-jerome-in-the-wi.scene: Unfinished: the gaunt saint kneels in the desert with the stone he beats his breast with, the lion stretched out before him.

el-greco-saint-jerome.webp.subject: saint-jerome
el-greco-saint-jerome.webp.scene: Jerome as a penitent hermit, kneeling naked at the mouth of a cave with his Bible in one hand and the stone he beat his breast with in the other.

caravaggio-saint-jerome-writing.webp.subject: saint-jerome
caravaggio-saint-jerome-writing.webp.scene: The old saint stretches across the table to dip his pen, his bald head echoed by a skull on the book opposite.

caravaggio-saint-jerome-writing-valletta.subject: saint-jerome
caravaggio-saint-jerome-writing-valletta.scene: Painted in Malta for the knights; Jerome writes beside a candle and skull, and the coat of arms of the knight who commissioned it is on the wall.

botticelli-the-last-communion-of-saint-j.subject: saint-jerome
botticelli-the-last-communion-of-saint-j.scene: Jerome, dying, is held up in his cell to receive his last communion.

botticelli-saint-augustine-in-his-study..subject: saint-augustine
botticelli-saint-augustine-in-his-study..scene: A fresco in the church of Ognissanti in Florence: Augustine looks up from his books at the moment of his vision of Jerome's death. Ghirlandaio painted Jerome as its pair.

botticelli-saint-augustine-in-his-cell.w.subject: saint-augustine
botticelli-saint-augustine-in-his-cell.w.scene: A small panel of Augustine writing in a vaulted cell, with torn drafts on the floor.

el-greco-saint-martin-and-the-beggar.web.subject: saint-martin
el-greco-saint-martin-and-the-beggar.web.scene: Martin, in gilded armour on a white horse, cuts his green cloak for the naked beggar. Toledo lies below.

subject: madonna
saint-martina
saint-agnes
el-greco-madonna-and-child-with-saint-ma.scene: Painted for the same chapel as Saint Martin and the Beggar: the Virgin in glory with angels, and below Martina with her lion and Agnes with her lamb.

el-greco-saint-ildefonso.webp.subject: saint-ildefonso
el-greco-saint-ildefonso.webp.scene: Ildefonso as a scholar at his desk, pausing in his writing to look at a statue of the Virgin, as if for inspiration.

caravaggio-saint-catherine-of-alexandria.subject: saint-catherine
caravaggio-saint-catherine-of-alexandria.scene: Catherine kneels against the broken, spiked wheel with the sword of her execution and the palm of martyrdom. The model is thought to be the courtesan Fillide Melandroni.

caravaggio-the-burial-of-saint-lucy.webp.subject: saint-lucy
caravaggio-the-burial-of-saint-lucy.webp.scene: Painted in Syracuse, Lucy's own city: two huge gravediggers dig her grave as the bishop blesses her body and the mourners stand against a vast bare wall.

caravaggio-the-martyrdom-of-saint-ursula.subject: saint-ursula
caravaggio-the-martyrdom-of-saint-ursula.scene: Probably Caravaggio's last painting: the Hun king has just shot Ursula at close range, and she looks down at the arrow in her breast. The face behind her is thought to be Caravaggio's.

stillman-saint-barbara.webp.subject: saint-barbara
stillman-saint-barbara.webp.scene: Barbara holds a model of her tower, its three windows showing the Trinity she believed in.

gentileschi-mary-magdalene-in-ecstasy.we.subject: mary-magdalene-legend
gentileschi-mary-magdalene-in-ecstasy.we.scene: The Magdalene leans back in a chair, eyes closed, in the trance of her desert years.

caravaggio-saint-francis-of-assisi-in-ec.subject: saint-francis
caravaggio-saint-francis-of-assisi-in-ec.scene: Caravaggio's first religious painting: Francis swoons after receiving the stigmata, held in the arms of an angel.

caravaggio-saint-francis-in-prayer.webp.subject: saint-francis
caravaggio-saint-francis-in-prayer.webp.scene: Francis kneels in prayer contemplating a skull. Wikipedia calls the Rome picture Saint Francis in Prayer and the Cremona one Saint Francis in Meditation; the titles are used both ways.
caravaggio-saint-francis-in-prayer.webp.uncertain: The two Saint Francis titles are swapped in some sources (see CLAUDE.md).

caravaggio-saint-francis-in-meditation.w.subject: saint-francis
caravaggio-saint-francis-in-meditation.w.scene: Francis meditates over a skull, a crucifix beside him.
caravaggio-saint-francis-in-meditation.w.uncertain: The two Saint Francis titles are swapped in some sources (see CLAUDE.md).

stillman-how-the-virgin-mary-came-to-bro.subject: brother-conrad
stillman-how-the-virgin-mary-came-to-bro.scene: In an Italian landscape the Virgin lays the Child in the friar's arms, while Brother Peter watches from among the trees.

caravaggio-the-martyrdom-of-saint-matthe.subject: saint-matthew
caravaggio-the-martyrdom-of-saint-matthe.scene: A naked executioner strikes down the old apostle at the altar, the congregation scatters, and an angel reaches down a palm. The bearded man looking back from the left is Caravaggio himself.

caravaggio-the-inspiration-of-saint-matt.subject: saint-matthew
caravaggio-the-inspiration-of-saint-matt.scene: An angel above counts off on his fingers as Matthew writes his Gospel, one knee on a stool that tips toward us. The first version, showing Matthew as a rough labourer guided by the angel's hand, was rejected and destroyed in Berlin in 1945.

caravaggio-crucifixion-of-saint-peter.we.subject: saint-peter
caravaggio-crucifixion-of-saint-peter.we.scene: Three labourers strain to raise the cross with the old apostle nailed upside down, as he asked.

caravaggio-the-crucifixion-of-saint-andr.subject: saint-andrew
caravaggio-the-crucifixion-of-saint-andr.scene: Painted in Naples for the Spanish viceroy: Andrew hangs on the cross after his prayer, and the executioner trying to untie him stands helpless, as the legend tells.

michelangelo-the-torment-of-saint-anthon.subject: saint-anthony
michelangelo-the-torment-of-saint-anthon.scene: Based on Schongauer's engraving, probably painted by Michelangelo at twelve or thirteen: demons lift Anthony into the air and tear at him. Vasari says the boy studied fish at the market to paint their scales.
michelangelo-the-torment-of-saint-anthon.uncertain: The attribution to Michelangelo is accepted by the Kimbell Art Museum but still debated.

botticelli-four-scenes-from-the-early-li.subject: saint-zenobius
botticelli-four-scenes-from-the-early-li.scene: Zenobius refuses the bride chosen for him, is baptized with his mother, and is consecrated bishop.

botticelli-three-miracles-of-saint-zenob.subject: saint-zenobius
botticelli-three-miracles-of-saint-zenob.scene: Three miracles in a Florentine street, among them the saint raising a dead child.

botticelli-three-miracles-of-saint-zenob.subject: saint-zenobius
botticelli-three-miracles-of-saint-zenob.scene: Three more miracles of the bishop, the panel now in the Met.

botticelli-the-last-miracle-and-the-deat.subject: saint-zenobius
botticelli-the-last-miracle-and-the-deat.scene: The bishop's last miracle and his death.

waterhouse-saint-eulalia.webp.subject: saint-eulalia
waterhouse-saint-eulalia.webp.scene: The girl lies dead in the snow of the forum, seen from above, with doves round her and a cross behind.

burne-jones-the-merciful-knight.webp.subject: merciful-knight
burne-jones-the-merciful-knight.webp.scene: The figure of Christ leans down from the wayside cross to embrace the kneeling knight in armour.

caravaggio-death-of-the-virgin.webp.subject: death-of-the-virgin
caravaggio-death-of-the-virgin.webp.scene: Mary lies dead on a bier, her feet swollen and bare, surrounded by the grieving apostles. The Carmelite friars who ordered it rejected it; Rubens persuaded the Duke of Mantua to buy it.

caravaggio-madonna-di-loreto.webp.subject: madonna-of-loreto
caravaggio-madonna-di-loreto.webp.scene: Two barefoot pilgrims kneel at a doorway before the Virgin and Child. The dirty soles of the pilgrim's feet scandalised some in Rome.

caravaggio-madonna-of-the-rosary.webp.subject: madonna-of-the-rosary
caravaggio-madonna-of-the-rosary.webp.scene: The Madonna directs Saint Dominic to give rosaries to the poor who press round him; the man in the ruff at the left is the patron.

saxon-saint-bartholomew.webp.subject: saint-bartholomew
saxon-saint-bartholomew.webp.scene: An enamel plaque of the apostle Bartholomew.

saxon-otto-i-presents-magdeburg-cathedra.subject: otto-magdeburg
saxon-otto-i-presents-magdeburg-cathedra.scene: One of a set of ivories made for Magdeburg Cathedral: the emperor, guided by Saint Maurice, offers a model of the cathedral to Christ.

rossetti-joan-of-arc.webp.subject: joan-of-arc
rossetti-joan-of-arc.webp.scene: Joan kisses the sword of deliverance. One of Rossetti's last pictures, finished a few days before he died in 1882.

rubens-head-of-one-of-the-three-kings-me.subject: magi
rubens-head-of-one-of-the-three-kings-me.scene: A study of one of the three kings, whom the Golden Legend names Caspar, Melchior and Balthasar.

botticelli-the-birth-of-venus.webp.subject: venus
botticelli-the-birth-of-venus.webp.scene: Venus, newly born from the sea, stands on a scallop shell blown ashore by Zephyr and the breeze Aura, while one of the Hours runs to cover her with a flowered cloak.

botticelli-primavera.webp.subject: primavera
botticelli-primavera.webp.scene: Read from right to left: Zephyr, Chloris becoming Flora, Venus with Cupid above her, the dancing Graces, and Mercury chasing away the clouds.

botticelli-venus-and-mars.webp.subject: venus
botticelli-venus-and-mars.webp.scene: Venus lies awake and watchful while Mars sleeps exhausted, so deeply that the little satyrs playing with his armour and blowing a conch in his ear cannot wake him: love conquers war. The wasps' nest by his head may be a pun on the Vespucci family, who may have commissioned it.

botticelli-pallas-and-the-centaur.webp.subject: pallas-and-centaur
botticelli-pallas-and-the-centaur.webp.scene: Pallas, crowned with olive and holding a great halberd, takes the centaur by the hair, and he submits.

botticelli-the-calumny-of-apelles.webp.subject: calumny
botticelli-the-calumny-of-apelles.webp.scene: Botticelli follows Lucian's description figure by figure: the king with ass's ears, Ignorance and Suspicion at his ears, Envy leading Slander, who drags her victim by the hair, Malice and Deceit dressing her hair, and at the left old Repentance turning to naked Truth, who points to heaven.

botticelli-fortitude.webp.subject: virtues
botticelli-fortitude.webp.scene: Fortitude sits enthroned in armour with her mace across her knees, Botticelli's first documented public work, painted in 1470.

botticelli-venus-and-the-three-graces-pr.subject: liberal-arts
botticelli-venus-and-the-three-graces-pr.scene: Venus and the Graces approach a young woman who holds out a cloth to receive their gift.

botticelli-a-young-man-being-introduced-.subject: liberal-arts
botticelli-a-young-man-being-introduced-.scene: A young man is led by the hand into the circle of the seven Arts, seated round Lady Philosophy, or Rhetoric.

bellini-the-infant-bacchus.webp.subject: bacchus
bellini-the-infant-bacchus.webp.scene: The child god stands in a landscape holding a jug of wine.

caravaggio-young-sick-bacchus.webp.subject: bacchus
caravaggio-young-sick-bacchus.webp.scene: An early self-portrait as Bacchus, painted, according to an early biographer, in a mirror while Caravaggio was recovering from illness; his skin and lips have a greenish tinge.

caravaggio-bacchus.webp.subject: bacchus
caravaggio-bacchus.webp.scene: A plump young god, crowned with vine leaves, holds out a goblet of wine to us. A tiny self-portrait of the painter at his easel has been found reflected in the wine carafe.

rome-sarcophagus-triumph-of-dionysos.web.subject: bacchus
rome-sarcophagus-triumph-of-dionysos.web.scene: The god rides a panther in procession, surrounded by satyrs and maenads. The four figures standing on the front are the Seasons.

bellini-the-feast-of-the-gods.webp.subject: feast-of-the-gods
bellini-the-feast-of-the-gods.webp.scene: The gods picnic in a wood; at the right Priapus lifts the dress of the sleeping Lotis, and the donkey on the left is about to bray. Titian later repainted the landscape to match his own pictures for the same room.

el-greco-laocoon.webp.subject: laocoon
